articles.title: 6 Common Phrases You May Not Realize Are Condescending
articles.summary: Experts explain what these phrases imply — and why you often use them without realizing their impact.
articles.body:
While we may strive to be kind and compassionate in our communications with people, we're bound to fall short sometimes. And one of the ways we do that in conversation? When we condescend, or talk down, to the other person.

We're being condescending when we speak to someone in a way that implies our own superiority, said journalist Celeste Headlee , author of "We Need to Talk: How to Have Conversations That Matter."

"It generally involves some kind of haughty tone, but condescension also almost always involves a passive-aggressive behavior," Headleetold HuffPost.

"In other words, when you are condescending to someone as in, 'Bless your heart,' you are putting on a false persona of kindness but beneath that is that clear message of superiority. You're treating them in a way that shows that they are an inferior."

Like this article? Keep independent journalism alive. Support HuffPost .

The tendency to talk down to others may have to do with trying to elevate our own social status, Headlee suggested.

"Our survival has always depended on our rank, our status, within a community," she said. "We need to be in a safe place within a community because it is through belonging — it is through community — that human beings survive."

Every conversation we have involves "impression management" in one way or another, she explained, "meaning that we are constantly managing the impression that we make on others."

"So people condescend because it's a way — whether it be conscious or not — that we can establish our rank above another person," she said.

According to Southern California psychotherapist Elisabeth Crain , speaking to others in a condescending manner can often be "traced back to underlying insecurity or an inflated ego," though she acknowledges this also happens when a person is just having a bad day and isn't cognizant of how they're coming off.

We all slip up from time to time, but generally we want to avoid communicating in a condescending way because it's insulting and demeaning to the other person.

"Nobody likes being condescended to. No one likes being told, 'You're of lower rank than I am,' or 'I'm superior to you,' which is essentially the underlying message of condescension," Headlee said.

And secondly, it's just not an effective way of getting our point across.

"The person on the receiving end is left with a bunch of feelings about the way the information has been presented, rather than the information itself," Crain said. "That, in and of itself, is a reason people should avoid talking in a condescending manner. They're going to lose their messaging and lose the efficacy of what they're trying to get across to others."

Condescension can also show up not just in what we say, but the tone of voice we employ, as well as nonverbal cues like facial expressions — e.g., rolling our eyes — or body language like patting someone on the head.

Here are some commonly used condescending phrases we may be saying without realizing their impact. (And keep in mind that what's condescending to one person may not be to another. It'a not a one-size-fits-all thing, Headlee pointed out.)

Other variations, including "that's sweet" or the Southern "bless your heart," can also come across as condescending. If you're genuinely trying to express that something is cute or sweet, that's fine. But be mindful of when you're using a tone of superiority, Crain said.

"'That's cute' can come off as belittling," she explained. "It's also not appropriate or helpful to label things like someone's understanding of something or effort to try to do something as 'cute.'"

Headlee offered another example: Say a friend is telling you about their boyfriend, but you don't really like the guy. Your friend shares a story and you respond with, "Oh, that's so sweet" in a patronizing kind of way.

"If you were in that situation, if you were telling a friend about their new boyfriend, what would you want to hear from that friend?" she said. "Even if they didn't like them, you'd probably want to hear something like, 'I'm so glad. It sounds like you found somebody you really like and that makes me really happy. I want you to be happy.'"

2. 'Well, actually...' (or other mansplaining verbiage)

Mansplaining is one of the more common examples of condescension, Headlee said.

It's "when you explain something to somebody that they either are already an expert in or that doesn't really need to be explained, that they clearly know," she said. "You often use really simplified language."

Phrasing may differ based on the situation, but a man chiming into a conversation with a woman to say "well, actually" and proceeding to lecture her on something obvious or something she already knows a great deal about is a classic example.

Of course, if someone asks you a direct question or says they don't know a term or recognize a concept, then go ahead and briefly fill them in.

Again, the tone behind the words is really important here.

"At times, this can be a genuine consolation, but it can also be patronizing, especially if the tone doesn't match the sentiment," writer Phoebe Mertens notes on Bolde.com. "It can sound like they've set low expectations and are surprised that the person managed to meet even those."

Think of it this way, Headlee said: If you were opening up to a friend about how you've been looking for a job and the search has been really tough, how would you feel if they responded with, "Well, sounds like you're trying your best."

"What would you want to hear in that situation? You'd probably want to hear something like, 'God that sounds tough. It's so rough to be looking for a job and not able to find one. You must be worried. Is there anything I could do to help?'" she said. "It's always just about figuring out what you would want to hear in the situation."

Giving someone definitive advice on how to live their life sure has a way of coming off as condescending.

"For example, saying, 'You should really do that; it would make your life so much better' or 'You must do that; you have to do this,'" Crain said.

Saying things this way "implies that the person's current way is wrong" and that you know better, Crain said.

Even making a small tweak to your approach can help. Consider something like: "'I think it could be helpful for you to do that,' rather than, 'You have to' or 'You should.' Maybe try using 'perhaps,'" Crain said.

"Anything that suggests a definitive way of doing things can be perceived as condescending because it puts pressure on the message. 'Perhaps' softens that pressure," she added.

This kind of response is both minimizing and invalidating, Oregon psychologist Scott Rower told HuffPost. It implies that just because you don't think it's important, the other person shouldn't either, discounting their experience and feelings on the matter.

"Whether you as the speaker think their feelings are disproportionate to the situation doesn't change that the person is feeling these feelings," Rower said. "Feelings are not chosen. The best way to keep these feelings active and someone stuck in them is to shame them for feeling them. Like the old phrase says, 'What we resist persists.'"

Or it might be phrased like, "You wouldn't get it" or "You don't get it, do you?"

"These phrases imply that the person on the receiving end isn't smart enough to figure something out or understand an experience that's not their own," Crain said.

And a final thought: Being condescending isn't something that only inconsiderate people do. We all make these kinds of mistakes when speaking to others, Headlee said.

"Conversation is one of the most complicated and difficult tasks any of us engage in. When you are in true conversation with another person, meaning you're really listening to them and you're engaging, it takes up a vast amount of cognitive power," she explained.

"You will say the wrong thing or someone will misinterpret your tone, so be prepared for it," she continued. "Be ready to be corrected and see it as just a growth opportunity between the both of you."

The original version of this story was published on HuffPost at an earlier date.

articles.title: Flood-hit Nepal sees child-trafficking risk rise; 102 children in camps without families
articles.summary: South Asia News: Flood-hit Nepal faces heightened child-trafficking risk as 1,283 children live in relief camps and 102 are without family; NGOs plan checkposts and monitoring.
articles.body: DEHRADUN:The risk of child trafficking has risen sharply in flood-hit Nepal, where at least 1,283 children are living in relief camps and 102 have no family members with them, prompting anti-trafficking groups to plan road checkposts, identify vulnerable children and monitor camps in areas devastated by the Aug 26 flash floods. Unicef has separately said more than 22,000 children urgently need sanitation, hygiene and food assistance.Anti-trafficking activists said the exact number of children who lost their entire families in the disaster was still unclear, making early identification particularly important. Anjila Dahal, who has worked on anti-human trafficking for eight years, told TOI that the 2015 earthquake had shown how quickly trafficking patterns could shift after a disaster. “We saw a significant move from cross-border trafficking to internal trafficking, with children from affected areas being taken to Kathmandu and Pokhara and pushed into snack houses, spas and massage centres. That is why we are more vigilant this time,” she said.Dahal said her organisation, whose name was withheld because of safety concerns for field activists, was focusing on prevention rather than waiting for trafficking cases to emerge. “We need to reach vulnerable communities early and stop children from falling into trafficking in the first place. We are planning checkposts on connecting roads in Nuwakot and Kispang, as in 2015 disaster, we had rescued children from vehicles carrying relief material. We are also monitoring relief camps sheltering children who have been left alone,” she said, adding that the NGO was prepared to move the most vulnerable children to shelter homes until their safety was secured.At a relief camp in Betrawati near Trishuli, Nepal-based NGO Karmayog Foundation’s founder Saurab Rimal said around 55 people were staying there, including 20 children, of whom five had no family member looking after them. “The children are aged between four and 15. Teenagers understand something of what has happened, but the younger children keep crying for their missing parents. It is heartbreaking, and the trafficking threat has made the situation even worse,” Rimal said.KIN India, which works to prevent cross-border human trafficking, has also deployed activists in affected areas to identify vulnerable children. Representative Naveen Joshi said difficult terrain and disrupted connectivity had slowed data collection, but teams would continue gathering information and coordinate with authorities for protective measures.Rasuwa chief district officer Narendra Pariyar said local bodies were running relief camps with support from NGOs and that the administration was alert to trafficking risks. “Relief camps for survivors, including children, are being run with the required facilities, and the administration is fully aware of the trafficking risk and is taking steps to mitigate it,” he said.The heightened vigilance reflects lessons from Nepal’s 2015 earthquake, when displacement, family separation and economic distress created new opportunities for traffickers. Activists said the immediate challenge now was to identify children separated from relatives, verify guardianship and stop anyone from moving them out of affected areas without scrutiny.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: El Niño just leveled up to super status. Here’s what that means for the weather
articles.summary: An already-strong El Niño just turned super as the phenomenon crosses into unprecedented territory.
articles.body:
An already-strong El Niño just turned super as the phenomenon crosses into unprecedented territory.

The natural climate cycle has been strengthening at a breakneck pace since it was first declared in June and is stronger now than it's ever been on this date. And isn't done bulking up yet.

Forecasters have thought for months that El Niño would become very strong or "super" by this fall. The key measure of its strength has now crossed that threshold and will continue to soar higher.

As a refresher: El Niño is characterized by warmer - than - average water temperatures along the equator in the Pacific Ocean. The warmer water triggers corresponding shifts in the atmosphere that have a domino effect on weather patterns around the globe.

An active Pacific hurricane season that's churned out multiple threats for Hawaii , a hurricane-less Atlantic hurricane season to date and Indonesia's overwhelming wildfires are just a few effects of this very strong El Niño.

The stronger an El Niño is, the more likely it is to influence these types of weather patterns — but it doesn't guarantee more extreme impacts.

To capture El Niño's strength, National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration forecasters measure how far above normal sea surface temperatures are in a specific region of the Pacific, using a metric called the Niño 3.4 Relative Oceanic Niño Index, or RONI.

The latest weekly RONI value just hit 2.0 degrees Celsius, 3.6 degrees Fahrenheit, above average. This is the threshold for "very strong," the highest official category set by forecasters. That's also when El Niño gains its unofficial "super" moniker.

These weekly values from NOAA capture a reliable snapshot of El Niño's strength in real-time, which is crucial because of just how fast the event is gaining ground.

This time a year ago, a weak La Niña — El Niño's cool counterpart — was in place, and only a handful of other years have had such a rapid flip to a potent El Niño, including the strongest ever event from 1982 to 1983.

Even so, using the weekly values is a slight departure from the norm.

NOAA's most widely recognized strength metric is a three-month rolling average RONI. The rolling average's purpose is to smooth out choppy short-term changes in data in favor of capturing a cleaner long-term average; that value updates once a month.

This is how a climate record that dates back decades is built, but the delayed data means it'll take weeks for that reading to truly capture how super-sized El Niño is right now.

This isn't a normal event: In addition to being the strongest El Niño on record on this date, it's ultimately likely to become stronger than any event before it.

By the end of the year, El Niño has a 75% chance of peaking as the strongest event since records began in 1950, according to NOAA's latest forecast issued last week.

This year's El Niño is also happening in a much hotter world than previous record-setting events due to climate change. One look at sea surface temperatures from this year compared to past record events shows just how much fossil fuel pollution has rewritten the rules.

Climate change has literally changed the metric used to monitor El Niño. This event is the first to be captured by NOAA's aforementioned RONI, which was first implemented in February.

The old metric took sea surface temperatures at face value, but RONI subtracts out how much warmer the Pacific Ocean is because of climate change to get the "true" strength of El Niño.

Even so, this El Niño continues to clear hurdles in its pursuit of record-breaking strength later this fall or early this winter.

Winter is when El Niño is forecast to hit its peak strength and is also typically when its influence on global weather is most pronounced, but it's already left many calling cards behind this summer as it strengthened rapidly.

It was, and continues to be, a major factor in both the Atlantic and Pacific hurricane seasons. In the Atlantic, it's taken storm-killing wind shear to extreme levels and kept it there, even at what should be the busiest time of the season. That's created a record-long wait for the season's first hurricane.

El Niño has prevented that same type of wind shear over the exceptionally warm Pacific and activity exploded. Sixteen storms, including two Category 5 hurricanes, have formed and thrived in the eastern and central parts of the ocean so far, with Hawaii alone facing three tropical systems in less than a month.

Fourteen of those storms originated in the East Pacific, which, with two and a half months of the season still to come, will likely blow past its average seasonal storm total of 15.

Elsewhere, Indonesia is battling widespread wildfires and conditions could deteriorate further: El Niño years make the country drier than usual, which leaves plenty of tinder-dry vegetation for blazes to consume and limited rainfall to help fire crews tamp down ongoing activity.

El Niño also raises global average air temperatures above levels already being increased by climate change and was a factor in making this summer such a scorcher around the globe. This August was Earth's hottest on record and could mark the start of a record-breaking warm stretch that would likely culminate in a record-hot 2027 — and possibly 2026 — globally.

It's clear El Niño is already a major player, but it will hit its full stride in the months ahead, right on time to dictate winter weather across the US.

articles.title: Lost oyster beds rediscovered thanks to Gaelic and Scots language
articles.summary: Scientists searched for the inclusion of the Gaelic and Scots words for oyster or oysters in place-names around Scotland's coast.
articles.body:
Long lost oyster beds on the West Coast of Scotland have been rediscovered thanks to Gaelic and Scots language.

Scientists searched for the inclusion of the Gaelic words for oyster or oysters – eisir, eisirein and eisirean – and oyster habitats like sandy banks or tidal causeways in place names around Scotland's coast.

They then found an oyster bed that had not been previously documented, as well as confirming oysters could have been present at other sites on Mull and Islay.

Native oysters were once abundant in coastal European waters, including Scotland, but now only remnant populations are known to remain due to overharvesting and disease.

More stories from Glasgow & West Scotland

Ecology and wildlife experts hope to use the discoveries to help rebuild oyster populations in suitable coastal locations.

The recent findings marked the culmination of several years worth of hard work, titled Project Eisirean.

It is a collaboration between ecology and environment researchers, Gaelic and education experts at the University of Glasgow and local community organisations on the west coast of Scotland.

Dr Anna McGregor, an expert in coastal ecology and a lecturer at the University of Glasgow , had the original idea of locating oysters through traditional place-names, then applying scientific techniques to confirm oyster presence within them.

She explained: "This is a really exciting outcome, for a project that started off looking for the historic distribution of oysters along the West Coast.

"We thought that as native oysters are now really rare throughout Europe, is there a way to look where they used to be, using people's memory and understanding - that can come through place names.

"We found two areas with oyster in the name, both on Mull, and after about two years we found another one on Lewis. Then we broadened the search to look for habitat related names, like sand banks."

The group then examined those locations for factors like the sea bed and the level of the water flow.

Dr McGregor hopes the team can build on their findings through continued work with local communities in Islay and Mull, alongside oyster bed restoration and protection work in key areas.

The research team will now trial the feasibility of a mobile oyster hatchery, in the hope it could both supply oyster larvae to coastal communities and help rebuild oyster beds in various areas.

The first mobile hatchery is being trialled in Millport, with plans to trial more in the future.

Dr McGregor said: "What we are hopping is to connect knowledge of the past, where shellfish was an important part of people's diets, to future improvement.

"We want to look where shellfish used to be, where communities had a connection with them, and develop that again.

"A small scale hatchery like this [on Millport] can be sustainable on an island, and really help people to connect with them.

"Seeing oysters life cycle can help people understand why it's important to keep them in the wild, and then get the numbers back up to levels where we can harvest them for lots of purposes."

The Native Oyster Restoration Alliance – NORA – coordinates projects across Europe to enhance the restoration of flat oyster reefs.

Hein Sas, the secretary of NORA, said: "The Eisirean project can serve as an example for other projects on how cultural heritage can help to identify suitable restoration sites."

articles.title: Complexo Viário Maria do Carmo: trânsito muda em Aracaju | G1
articles.standfirst: Mudança acontece a partir desta quarta-feira (16).
articles.summary: O Complexo Viário Maria do Carmo terá novo fluxo para quem segue da Avenida Beira-Mar rumo à Tancredo Neves; agentes da SMTT orientam condutores nesta quarta (16).
articles.body:
Complexo Viário Maria do Carmo em Aracaju — Foto: Ascom/SMTT

A partir desta quarta-feira (16), os condutores que trafegam pela avenida Governador Paulo Barreto de Menezes (Beira-Mar), no sentido Atalaia-Centro com destino à avenida Tancredo Neves, em Aracaju , deverão utilizar a nova alça de acesso do Complexo Viário Maria do Carmo.

De acordo com a Superintendência Municipal de Transportes e Trânsito (SMTT), a nova alça, localizada após o viaduto, passa a concentrar o fluxo de veículos com destino à Avenida Tancredo Neves, modificando a circulação na região.

Com a alteração, o acesso que era feito antes do viaduto deixará de ser utilizado. Agentes da SMTT estarão no local para orientar os condutores durante a implantação da mudança.

articles.title: Obras alteram trânsito em rodovias do Sul de Minas; veja trechos | G1

articles.summary: Intervenções de pavimentação, sinalização e manutenção podem provocar Pare e Siga, estreitamento de pista e interdições temporárias até domingo (20).
articles.body:
Motoristas que vão circular pelas rodovias do Sul de Minas devem ficar atentos a obras e serviços de manutenção programados até domingo (20). As intervenções ocorrem em diferentes estradas da região e podem provocar Pare e Siga, estreitamento de pista, fechamento temporário de faixas e interdições pontuais.

Entre os serviços previstos estão recuperação e aplicação de asfalto, fresagem, manutenção de defensas metálicas, pintura de faixas, instalação de tachas refletivas, drenagem, recuperação de erosões e manutenção de pontes.

A programação pode sofrer alterações por causa das condições climáticas ou de necessidades operacionais. Nos trechos com interferência no trânsito, a orientação é reduzir a velocidade, respeitar a sinalização provisória e seguir as orientações das equipes que trabalham na pista.

Na BR-381, a Fernão Dias, equipes também reforçaram os serviços de recuperação do pavimento após as fortes chuvas registradas nos últimos dias.

As obras ocorrem em diferentes pontos da rodovia e podem provocar fechamentos temporários de faixas e interdições pontuais. A sinalização deve ser reforçada nos locais de trabalho.

Como dirigir nos trechos em obras ou com chuva

Reduza a velocidade ao se aproximar de áreas em obras.

Respeite a sinalização provisória e o Pare e Siga.

Aumente a distância em relação ao veículo da frente.

Em caso de chuva, evite freadas e mudanças bruscas de direção.

Fique atento a pontos com acúmulo de água e alterações no pavimento.

Mantenha os faróis acesos durante a viagem.

Evite parar no acostamento, que deve permanecer livre para situações de emergência.

Ao passar por equipes de manutenção ou veículos de atendimento, reduza a velocidade e, se houver segurança para isso, mude de faixa, mantendo distância dos trabalhadores.

articles.body:
Calor de Teresina — Foto: Pedro Victor/g1 Piauí

O Instituto Nacional de Meteorologia (Inmet) emitiu um alerta de baixa umidade para 188 municípios do Piauí nesta terça-feira (15). O aviso é válido das 10h às 22h, período em que a umidade relativa do ar deve ficar entre 20% e 30% nas áreas afetadas.

Além do alerta, três cidades piauienses registraram algumas das menores umidades do ar do país na segunda-feira (14), segundo o Inmet. Oeiras liderou o ranking nacional, com índice de 11%.

São João do Piauí também registrou umidade de 11%, enquanto Paulistana ficou com 12%, ocupando posições entre as cinco menores marcas do país no dia.

De acordo com o Inmet, o alerta é de perigo potencial. A condição pode aumentar o risco de incêndios florestais e causar problemas de saúde, como ressecamento da pele e desconforto nas vias respiratórias. Entre os municípios atingidos estão Teresina , Altos , Picos e Floriano.

Durante o período de baixa umidade, o Inmet orienta a população a beber bastante líquido, evitar atividades físicas intensas nos horários mais secos e reduzir a exposição ao sol nas horas mais quentes do dia.

Em caso de necessidade, o órgão recomenda buscar orientações junto à Defesa Civil, pelo telefone 199, e ao Corpo de Bombeiros, pelo número 193.

articles.title: Chuva de granizo em Goiás deixa paisagem branca em Chapadão do Céu | G1
articles.standfirst: Meteorologista André Amorim informou que Chapadão do Céu registrou 18mm em cerca de 20 minutos. A chuva de granizo foi causado pelo encontro de um calor extremo com uma frente fria que partiu do Mato Grosso do Sul.
articles.summary: Chuva de granizo em Goiás atingiu Chapadão do Céu após calor extremo. O fenômeno acumulou gelo em rodovias e foi registrado em vídeo por moradores da região.
articles.body:
Uma chuva de granizo em Chapadão do Céu, no sudoeste de Goiás, deixou a paisagem coberta de branco e impressionou moradores da região (veja o video acima). Nos vídeos registrados pelos moradores, é possível ver o chão todo branco, da beira da estrada até o horizonte da paisagem.

A chuva de granizo foi registrada no domingo (13). Ao g1 , Pamela Almeida contou que estava com a família na rodovia que liga Chapadão do Céu e Costa Rica, no Mato Grosso do Sul, no final da tarde, quando registrou as imagens. Ela estava indo com a família para casa em uma fazenda onde moram e contou que sua filhas ficaram encantadas.

"Elas ficaram encantada com o gelo, super animadas em verem essa cena", relatou.

Chuva de granizo deixa paisagem coberta de branco e impressiona em Goiás — Foto: Reprodução/TV Anhanguera

Segundo o gerente do Centro de Informações Meteorológicas e Hidrológicas de Goiás (Cimehgo), André Amorim, todas as regiões de Goiás registraram calor extremo, o que foi ao encontro de uma frente fria que partiu do Mato Grosso do Sul. O meteorologista informou que Chapadão do Céu registrou 18mm em cerca de 20 minutos.

"Uma chuva bem rápida de tempestade. No caso de Chapadão do Céu, algumas vezes o ar empurra as gotículas de água para o topo da nuvem, onde é mais frio, e essas gotículas começam a congelar e começam girando ali, porque tem vento dentro das nuvens. Elas vão aglutinando e ,em determinado momento, a chuva que viria em estado líquido acaba caindo em estado sólido", explicou.

articles.title: Vai pegar a estrada com chuva? Veja cuidados para evitar aquaplanagem | G1
articles.standfirst: Duas pessoas morreram após um carro aquaplanar e bater contra um caminhão na Rodovia João Mellão, em Avaré (SP). Aquaplanagem acontece quando os pneus perdem o contato com o asfalto por causa da água acumulada.
articles.summary: Após mortes na Rodovia João Mellão, especialistas orientam como prevenir a aquaplanagem em rodovias e os cuidados essenciais ao dirigir sob chuvas intensas.
articles.body:
A região de Itapetininga (SP) vem sendo afetada pelas fortes chuvas que atingem o estado de São Paulo desde quinta-feira (10). Em diferentes cidades, foram registrados casos de alagamentos, enchentes, pessoas desalojadas e interdições, inclusive em rodovias.

O excesso de água nas pistas de rodovias importantes para a circulação na região, como a Raposo Tavares (SP-270) e a João Mellão (SP-255), também aumenta o risco de aquaplanagem, quando os pneus perdem o contato com o asfalto por causa da água acumulada.

Na manhã de quinta-feira (10), um acidente envolvendo um caminhão e um carro causou duas mortes e deixou outras duas pessoas feridas em Avaré . Testemunhas relataram que o carro aquaplanou na pista devido à forte chuva .Chuva provoca alagamentos, deslizamentos de terra e interdições de rodovias na região de Itapetininga

Ao g1 , o engenheiro mecânico Luiz Giácomo conta que, há alguns anos, ele passou por uma situação do tipo. Por não saber como lidar com a aquaplanagem, acabou batendo o carro em que estava com a família em um barranco em uma via próxima à Itapetininga.

"Estava em uma chuva intensa e peguei um 'canal' na pista, que fez o carro aquaplanar. Eu estava com a velocidade abaixo do limite. O carro rodopiou, bateu no barranco e foi batendo diversas vezes. Meu filho precisou ser socorrido, mas não teve sequelas", lembra.

Segundo o profissional, os danos no carro foram grandes, caracterizando-o como "perda total". Depois disso, ele passou a utilizar da profissão que exerce como uma forma de tomar medidas preventivas para evitar acidentes do tipo.

"O carro amassou tudo que poderia ser amassado. Sou engenheiro mecânico e, a partir desse acidente, comecei a tomar medidas. Sempre oriento os amigos e falo para algumas pessoas quando perguntam sobre", diz.

Rodovias do sudoeste paulista registraram casos de aquaplanagem — Foto: SPVias/Divulgação

Luiz aponta que as orientações são uma série de cuidados considerados básicos, porém, essenciais na hora de pegar o volante em um dia de chuva. O primeiro passo é reduzir a velocidade.

"Eu sempre aconselho as pessoas a reduzirem para cerca de 70% da velocidade permitida na estrada, porque a velocidade é um fator importantíssimo para causar aquaplanagem", comenta.

Um segundo fator é o estado de conservação dos pneus . Com o desgaste ao passar do tempo, a parte externa acaba ficando "careca", ou seja, perdendo os sulcos que podem ajudar a expulsar a água do pneu em dias de chuva.

"Os sulcos, além de evitar a derrapagem, evita a água. Os sulcos expulsam aquela camada que fica por causa da aquaplanagem. É muito perigoso andar com um pneu 'careca'. Todos eles tem um sinal de vida, exatamente para evitar a derrapagem e a aquaplanagem. É importante trocar o pneu sempre que ele apresentar sinais de desgaste", pontua.

O alinhamento do pneu, segundo Luiz, também pode ser uma dica valiosa para evitar acidentes envolvendo a aquaplanagem. O veículo, quando desalinhado, perde o contato total com o asfalto, aumentando as chances e os riscos.

"O pneu pode estar novo, mas se ele não está alinhado e com um ângulo diferente do habitual, ele não tem contato total com o asfalto. A área de contato é muito pequena e pode causar acidentes também. Não só isso, mas aumentar a distância com o carro que está à sua frente, porque a eficiência da frenagem diminui com a água", acrescenta.

O engenheiro reforça que, caso um motorista tenha aquaplanado o carro, a orientação principal é não mexer o volante e manter a calma . Tentar desviar do local pode acabar fazendo com que o veículo fique descontrolado, gerando acidentes ainda piores.

"Não pode mexer no volante. Se você fizer isso, a probablidade do carro pegar o contato com o asfalto é maior ainda e pode acabar virando, perdendo o controle. Foi o que aconteceu comigo a hora que tentei acertar a direção. O certo é deixar ele aquaplanar até parar", ensina.

Chuvas de verão aumentam risco de aquaplanagem nas rodovias do interior de SP — Foto: Reprodução/TV TEM

Valquíria Ritter, coordenadora de operações da Motiva SPVias, concessionária responsável por grande parte das rodovias da região de Itapetininga, aponta que, em períodos chuvosos, todo cuidado é pouco ao transitar em rodovias. Assista ao vídeo no início da reportagem.

"Se chover durante o trajeto, reduza a velocidade, aumente a distância entre o veículo à sua frente, evite freadas e redobre a sua atenção. Mantenha os faróis baixos acesos e, antes de sair de casa, certifique-se de que os pneus e o para-brisa estão em bom funcionamento", reforça.

Verifique as condições dos pneus e das palhetas do para-brisa;

Reduza a velocidade e dirija com atenção redobrada;

Use os faróis baixos, mesmo durante o dia;

Mantenha distância segura do veículo à frente;

Evite freadas bruscas e mudanças repentinas de direção;

Redobre a atenção em trechos com acúmulo de água.

Duas pessoas morreram após um carro aquaplanar e bater de frente com um caminhão na Rodovia João Mellão, em Avaré (SP), na quinta-feira (10). Outras duas pessoas também ficaram feridas.

Segundo a Motiva SPVias, o acidente aconteceu no km 275 da pista sentido interior. Uma pessoa foi socorrida em estado grave e outra teve ferimentos moderados.

articles.title: Serra Antiga da Tamoios: interdição por chuva já dura 30 horas | G1
articles.standfirst: Pista está bloqueada desde 21h30 de domingo (13), após registro de deslizamento e queda de árvore. É a terceira interdição da serra em menos de uma semana.
articles.summary: Serra Antiga da Tamoios segue bloqueada devido aos riscos de deslizamento. Motoristas utilizam a Serra Nova em sistema de comboio enquanto a pista passa por limpeza.
articles.body:
Serra antiga da Rodovia dos Tamoios é interditada por causa do alto volume de chuva — Foto: Tamoios/Reprodução

A Serra Antiga da Rodovia dos Tamoios ultrapassou 30 horas de interdição nesta terça-feira (15) . A pista está fechada desde as 21h30 de domingo (13), quando a concessionária voltou a bloquear o trecho por causa das condições provocadas pelas chuvas. Até a manhã desta terça, ainda não havia previsão de liberação.

O fechamento ocorre como medida de segurança quando o volume de chuva e as condições da serra aumentam o risco de deslizamentos e quedas de árvores. Um dos critérios utilizados pela concessionária é o acumulado de 100 milímetros de chuva em 72 horas, mas a decisão também considera outros fatores observados no trecho.

Durante a interdição atual, houve um deslizamento de terra no km 73,4 e uma queda de árvore no km 77,9. Equipes trabalham na limpeza e na avaliação das condições da pista e das encostas antes de uma possível liberação.

Essa é a terceira interdição da Serra Antiga em menos de uma semana. O primeiro bloqueio ocorreu na quinta-feira (10) e durou cerca de 22 horas. Depois, a pista voltou a ser interditada no sábado (12), permanecendo fechada por aproximadamente 37 horas, até ser liberada às 15h de domingo (13). Seis horas e meia depois, às 21h30, o trecho foi novamente bloqueado.

Enquanto a Serra Antiga está fechada, o tráfego é direcionado para a Serra Nova, onde funciona a Operação Comboio com Pare e Siga. No sentido São José dos Campos , os veículos seguem em comboio; no sentido litoral, o tráfego é organizado por categorias de veículos.

A sequência de interdições acontece em um período de chuva frequente na região. Com o solo encharcado, a ocorrência de novos deslizamentos e quedas de árvores aumenta, e a concessionária mantém o monitoramento das condições da serra para definir quando o tráfego poderá ser retomado com segurança.

articles.title: MPT investiga possíveis irregularidades em comunidade terapêutica | G1
articles.standfirst: Apuração começou após inspeção que reuniu diferentes órgãos diante de relatos de possíveis violações de direitos humanos e trabalhistas.
articles.summary: Apuração começou após inspeção que reuniu diferentes órgãos diante de relatos de possíveis violações de direitos humanos e trabalhistas.
articles.body:
Comunidade terapêutica de MS é alvo de apuração do MPT — Foto: MPT

O Ministério Público do Trabalho em Mato Grosso do Sul (MPT-MS) abriu uma apuração para verificar possíveis irregularidades trabalhistas na Estância Terapêutica Efésios 6, em Três Lagoas (MS). A investigação começou após uma inspeção realizada na comunidade na quarta-feira (9).

O g1 tentou contato com a comunidade, mas não obteve retorno.

A fiscalização foi organizada pela Defensoria Pública de Mato Grosso do Sul e reuniu diferentes órgãos que atuam na proteção de direitos. O objetivo foi verificar relatos de possíveis violações de direitos humanos e também situações que poderiam estar relacionadas às condições de trabalho no local.

Durante a visita, a procuradora do Trabalho Cláudia Fernanda Noriler Silva e uma equipe do MPT recolheram documentos sobre as atividades realizadas na comunidade terapêutica.

Entre os materiais analisados estão termos de compromisso de estágio, documentos de adesão ao trabalho voluntário e um contrato de prestação de serviços.

Com base no que foi encontrado durante a inspeção e nos documentos recolhidos, o MPT registrou uma chamada "Notícia de Fato". Essa é a primeira etapa de uma apuração do órgão e serve para reunir informações antes de decidir se é necessário aprofundar a investigação.

Neste momento, ainda não há uma conclusão sobre a existência de irregularidades trabalhistas na instituição.

Depois da análise dos documentos e das demais informações, o procedimento poderá ser arquivado, caso não sejam encontradas situações que justifiquem a continuidade da apuração.

Se houver necessidade de investigar mais a fundo, o caso poderá ser transformado em um Procedimento Preparatório ou em um Inquérito Civil.

A inspeção foi realizada a convite da Defensoria Pública, por meio do Núcleo Institucional de Promoção e Defesa dos Direitos Humanos e do Núcleo de Atenção à Saúde.

Também participaram da ação representantes do Ministério Público Estadual, da Vigilância Sanitária Estadual, do Conselho Regional de Farmácia de Mato Grosso do Sul e do Ministério do Trabalho e Emprego, por meio da Auditoria Fiscal do Trabalho.

A atuação conjunta ocorreu diante de relatos sobre possíveis violações de direitos humanos e suspeitas de irregularidades trabalhistas na comunidade terapêutica.

Na mesma ocasião, outras duas comunidades terapêuticas também foram inspecionadas. O MPT, no entanto, não participou dessas duas fiscalizações.

A apuração sobre a Estância Terapêutica Efésios 6 segue em andamento.

articles.summary: O Vestibular Fatec oferece vagas em Mogi das Cruzes, Suzano e região com inscrições abertas até novembro para diversos cursos superiores gratuitos.

O vestibular das Faculdades de Tecnologia do Estado de São Paulo (Fatecs) já está com inscrições abertas. No total são 467 oportunidades distribuídas entre as unidades de Arujá , Ferraz de Vasconcelos , Itaquaquecetuba , Mogi das Cruzes e Suzano .

A inscrição deve ser feita pela internet, com o preenchimento da ficha e do questionário socioeconômico. O candidato pode escolher um curso como primeira opção e outro como segunda opção.

O pagamento da taxa pode ser feito em agências bancárias, internet banking ou cartão de crédito.

articles.title: Estudo monitora reprodução do caranguejo-uçá no Amapá | G1
articles.standfirst: Maior andada do caranguejo-uçá em 2026 ocorreu fora do período de defeso. O registro foi feito na Estação Ecológica Maracá-Jipioca (Esec), localizada no município de Amapá.
articles.summary: A maior andada reprodutiva do caranguejo-uçá em 2026 ocorreu fora do período de defeso, na Estação Ecológica Maracá-Jipioca (ESEC), localizada no município de Amapá.
articles.body:
A maior andada reprodutiva do caranguejo-uçá em 2026 ocorreu fora do período de defeso , na Estação Ecológica Maracá-Jipioca (Esec) , localizada no município de Amapá. Pesquisadores do projeto Costamar registraram o fenômeno no mês de agosto .

A descoberta indica que o calendário atual não protege toda a fase reprodutiva da espécie . O estudo reúne dados que podem contribuir para a revisão e a definição de uma nova política adequada ao ciclo reprodutivo do caranguejo-uçá no estado.

De acordo com Jonas Rosa, supervisor regional do Projeto Costamar, ainda não há explicação para as andadas fora do período previsto .

“A andada é o período em que machos e fêmeas saem para procurar um parceiro sexual. Nós identificamos essa andada fora do defeso, e a captura durante esse período pode prejudicar a reprodução, os estoques e a comercialização do animal”, disse.

Pesquisadores do projeto realizam monitoramentos a cada 15 dias na estação ecológica. Uma das hipóteses considera que fatores ambientais do estado, como o clima e os manguezais, influenciam o período das andadas.

Caranguejo-uçá também é conhecido como catanhão, caranguejo-verdadeiro e uçaúna — Foto: Divulgação

O comportamento dos animais também muda de um ano para o outro . A pesquisa deve durar três anos para ampliar os dados e identificar um padrão de reprodução no Amapá.

Em outros estados, o estudo já foi realizado, e os resultados contribuíram para a definição de novos períodos de defeso.

O período de defeso protege determinadas espécies durante fases importantes do ciclo reprodutivo . Nesse intervalo, a legislação estabelece restrições à pesca e à comercialização para permitir a reprodução dos animais e contribuir para a renovação dos estoques. As regras de defeso variam conforme a espécie e a região .

Proteção ambiental: o defeso pode proibir ou restringir a captura, o transporte e a comercialização de determinadas espécies durante o período de reprodução.

Exceções: a legislação pode permitir a pesca de subsistência para comunidades tradicionais e ribeirinhas , dentro de limites específicos de quantidade e equipamentos.

Seguro-Defeso: pescadores profissionais artesanais que atendem aos requisitos legais podem receber um benefício financeiro durante o período em que ficam impedidos de exercer a atividade.

Penalidades: quem descumpre as regras do defeso pode cometer crime ambiental e ter equipamentos e produtos apreendidos, além de receber multas.

articles.title: Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire
articles.summary: The state post service delivers pensions, medicine and letters to people just miles from the front.
articles.body:
Every morning Igor Smelyansky looks at a vast map of Ukraine on his office wall and decides where he should put his people in harm's way.

His aides provide him with live intelligence about Russian attacks and he deploys his teams, balancing their potential operational success against risk to life or limb.

But Smelyansky is no military commander. He is the head of Ukraine's state postal service, Ukrposhta.

And every day he must decide how far to send his postmen and women into the deadly "kill zone" along the front lines where the threat of drone attack is ever present.

"If it's too dangerous to go today, we won't go," Smelyansky told us. "We'll go tomorrow, or we'll go somewhere else. The key is to be as agile as you can."

Ukrposhta does more than just collect letters and parcels. It pays out pensions in hard cash, it takes payment for utility bills. And it delivers vital food and medicine to people on the margins of society.

As such, it offers a lifeline to millions of poor and elderly Ukrainians living in remote villages where shops are rare and trips to the city are expensive and dangerous. In a vast rural nation wracked by war, Ukrposhta is part of the glue that holds the country together.

That has made the service a target for Russia - which in recent months has stepped up not only its attacks on postmen and women but also sorting offices and logistical hubs. The Kremlin has claimed strikes like this are retaliation for Ukrainian attacks on Russian online retailers like Wildberries.

Speaking in his imposing Soviet-era office building that overlooks Kyiv's famous Maidan square, Smelyansky said: "If we don't go [to a village], we don't have basic supply. We don't have food. We don't have medicine. People will struggle. If we do go, they may delay a decision to evacuate from the areas they probably should have evacuated."

There are many risks. If a post van turns up unannounced, a crowd can form, creating a target for an opportunistic Russian drone operator. But if they call ahead, information could leak.

"Is it a danger?" Smelyansky said. "Absolutely. Because there are Russian sympathisers who can give them the location of the truck that's coming."

If Smelyansky chooses not to send a van in, he faces criticism. "You get messages from people from those villages: 'You betrayed us. You didn't come...' But if I go, I may risk the life of the driver."

Smelyansky says Russia is deliberately targeting his staff because of the vital role they play shoring up Ukraine's resilience, helping people stay alive in their homes through the fighting and bitter winters.

"It's not an accident, it's deliberate," he said. "By attacking Ukrposhta, you put pressure on people… who are depending on the truck coming in." Russia denies targeting civilians.

Since 2022, hundreds of Ukrposhta branches and vehicles have been hit, and more than 50 staff have lost their lives, either on the frontline or on their rounds, according to Ukrposhta.

We travelled with Kateryna Marynych, a 38-year-old postmistress, near Zaporizhzhia - a city not too far from the southern frontlines.

She lost her home and her husband during the full-scale invasion, and came to the area to rebuild her life. She ran the post office in the village of Lukasheve for two years until it was destroyed in March by a Russian drone, targeting soldiers working nearby.

After her van drew up, a steady queue of elderly folk formed. She sat in the front passenger seat, window open, handing out cash, taking payments.

One customer, Nadiia, said she was grateful: "It's a long way for us to travel to Zaporizhzhia. Especially now, at a time when there are attacks all around us. The fact that they come here is really nice."

Oleksandrivna, 77, arrived wearing a purple dressing gown, walking with a crutch. When I asked her where she would be without Kateryna, she replied: "We would be stuffed! I am just out of hospital after a stroke. Where could I go for my medicine?"

But Mykola, 64, pointed to another service the post office provides to a largely elderly population. "It is very important," he said. "It's one of the few joys of the month: you come out, have a chat with people, collect your pension, and go home."

For many people in remote communities, Kateryna can be their last link with the Ukrainian state.

She says she hopes her customers are proud of her. "They love me, they need me," she said. "They are waiting for me. Sometimes they call me, especially after attacks on Zaporizhzhia and ask me how I am. We are like a big family. My attitude towards them is like a grandmother or grandfather."

The attacks on Ukrposhta form part of Russia's wider escalation of its war on Ukraine, stepping up fast drone attacks on civilian infrastructure including business infrastructure, energy facilities, transport networks and border posts. Analysts say that as Russia's invasion stagnates on the battlefield in the east, it is looking for other ways of putting pressure on Kyiv.

For safety, Kateryna always travels with her partner, Slava, who drives. While she sorts the cash, he works from the back of the van, taking and receiving parcels, delivering food and water. He also carries a side-arm in a holster, for personal protection; these vans carry a lot of cash.

Both wear body armour when close to the front line. And they have an antenna in the van that shows them the location of the small first-person-view drones that render the frontline so deadly. They have seen drones from the car but luckily have not yet been hit.

She accepted her job was dangerous but would never change it. "It is my work," she said. "If I can't, who will do my job?"

Ukraine's defence comes in many forms - and it's not always delivered at the barrel of a gun.

articles.title: Charities praise will gifts amid 'affordability challenges'
articles.summary: Jersey charities say leaving donations in wills can be "transformational", regardless of how much.
articles.body:
People who leave charities donations, legacies and bequests in their wills make noticeable differences to organisations, no matter what the amount is, sector leaders say.

The comments come as one leader acknowledged living costs could present "affordability challenges" for potential givers.

Marcus Liddiard, from the Association of Jersey Charities, said, despite "the number of people giving is very, very high compared to the UK", it was "hard to tell" how the cost of living might affect giving.

The chair of Jersey Fundraising Forum, Bethany Gallichan, said she understood some people were struggling, but added any money left in wills could be "transformational".

Research carried out for the Association of Jersey Charities by 4insight found 89% of respondents had given money in the previous 12 months, but younger people and lower-income households were less likely to have donated, with affordability being a "key barrier".

Liddiard said, despite this, legacy giving remained important, and people needed to amounts left in wills did not have to be headline-grabbing.

He said: "The ones you hear about often can be the really big ones, but some of most impactful ones are the smaller everyday ones".

He added legacy giving was "one part" of the picture and there was also "opportunity for everybody" to also help by volunteering and offering time, skills, representation and support, which was "equally valuable".

Gallichan added: "I do understand people are struggling with the cost of living crisis, but we do have people who have the ability to leave those gifts, and they can be so transformational, especially to those charitable organisations that are seeing costs rising and services in higher demand".

She added such gifts could help fund services for islanders struggling with the cost of living.

Jersey Trees for Life said legacy donations made "a huge difference" to it.

It was gifted land at Adelina Wood by Enid Gautier last year, plus Mont Vibert Wood, as well as £20,000 by islanders who passed away.

John Michel, from the charity, said it was "very special" to be recognised in wills and it was "really quite inspiring when someone local" made what could be a "transformational" move.

Karla Summers-Shaw, from law firm Viberts, said it was "really easy" for anyone to leave a legacy.

"The size of the gift is completely proportionate to the size of a person's estate, and I always say no gift is too small," she said.

articles.title: Reading for pleasure can improve wellbeing, Cambridge study finds
articles.summary: University of Cambridge academics say reading at any age improves brain and mental health.
articles.body:
Reading for pleasure can improve health and wellbeing at any age and regardless of what you read, University of Cambridge academics have said.

Prof Barbara Sahakian and Dr Christelle Langley, from the university's department of psychiatry, argued that reading boosts mental health and academic performance, leading to greater empathy and lowering the risk of dementia.

Their review, published in the journal Psychological Medicine, found reading at any age improves brain and mental health, enhances cognitive performance and reduces the risk of mental decline.

Sahakian added that "it's never too late to start" reading, as "it can bring benefits throughout our lives and into old age".

Langley said: "Given how beneficial reading for pleasure is at a young age, we should be doing everything we can to introduce children and young people to reading.

"The important thing is to find something they'd really enjoy reading about – it might be a TV programme or a game – and use this as a way in."

The Cambridge scientists worked with The Queen's Reading Room – the charity founded by Queen Camilla to highlight the benefits of reading – as part of the National Year of Reading.

As part of the review, one study involving more than 10,000 young people found that children who begin reading for pleasure early in life have a better attention span, memory and problem-solving skills.

The researchers said those children tend to perform better at school, have fewer mental health problems, and lead healthier lifestyles – including more sleep and less screen time.

Sahakian said book clubs or reading groups also "provide additional benefits through social interaction".

"They can help people feel less isolated and more connected to others, which has been shown to reduce the risk of dementia," she added.

The review also found adults aged 55 and older who were engaged in activities such as reading were significantly less likely to develop cognitive impairment.

articles.title: Why is Piddington in Oxfordshire holding a referendum on leaving the UK?
articles.summary: Residents of Piddington, near Bicester, will vote in a symbolic referendum on Tuesday.
articles.body:
Residents of a small village set to house more than 1,000 asylum seekers are due to vote in a symbolic referendum on whether it should remain part of the UK.

Piddington, a village of about 400 people near Bicester in Oxfordshire, decided in July to hold the vote after the government announced plans to house asylum seekers at a nearby Ministry of Defence (MoD) site.

Under the proposal, MoD Bicester could be converted into basic accommodation to house up to 1,256 male asylum seekers.

The Home Office said it was "working to fairly house asylum seekers across the country" and that it had saved taxpayers over £1bn on asylum support costs since the election.

The vote is taking place on Tuesday – but why is it being held, and will it make any difference?

The Home Office announced the plans in June as part of wider proposals to move people out of hotels.

Known as "Site A", MoD Bicester is located between the villages of Piddington and Upper and Lower Arncott.

In 2005 it was the target of similar plans for an asylum seekers accommodation centre , which were abandoned by the then-Labour government.

This year's announcement sparked widespread criticism, including from the district council and human rights groups, with many residents expressing shock.

Chair of Piddington Parish Council Tim McNally said he was fearful over "security".

Piddington falls within the constituency of Lib Dem MP for Bicester, Calum Miller. He previously said the plans had been "veiled in secrecy" and that the process did not guarantee public participation "beyond a narrow list of statutory bodies".

However, earlier this month the government published an Urgent Crown Development application .

Miller called it a "clear win for local democracy and for every resident who refused to be shut out of a decision with profound consequences for our communities".

A public consultation on the plans is now running until midnight on 17 September.

There is no legal mechanism allowing a village, town or city to declare independence from the UK.

Therefore, a village holding a referendum can only be symbolic, which is what the one held in Piddington will be. It has been organised by Piddington Parish Council, following a vote supporting the idea.

McNally previously said the referendum would be an attempt to make voices in the village heard.

Ahead of the vote, about 20 women gathered at the village green on Monday to meet shadow home secretary Chris Philp, shadow minister for women and equalities Joy Morrissey, and Reform UK MPs Sarah Pochin and Suella Braverman.

Pochin and Braverman were among the MPs to respond to an open letter penned by a group of Piddington's female residents, addressed to all women MPs.

In the letter, the group of 133 women said they faced a "crisis" and argued their "safety, security and freedoms will be under threat".

"Life as we know it will be destroyed," they said.

"We will not feel safe walking our streets. We are already living in fear."

In a statement regarding the letter, the Home Office previously said the "concerns of communities" were central to its immigration reforms.

"That is why we are closing every asylum hotel and moving asylum seekers into alternative accommodation, including former military sites," a spokesperson said.

Gloria Brown, 69, who has lived in Piddington for 23 years, said she would stop litter-picking in the village if plans went ahead, something she takes "lots of pride" in doing.

"All my friends in the village call me Madame Cholet," Ms Brown said. "I wouldn't be able to do that anymore. I do it on my own sometimes."

She added: "How ever am I going to get my mental health back to scale? Because it's going to make me feel imprisoned in my own village.

"I've felt very emotional about it just lately, and it's just not correct, and it's totally unfair."

A Home Office spokesperson said: "The government is closing every asylum hotel, saving taxpayers over £1bn on asylum support since the election.

"We are working to fairly house asylum seekers across the country, moving asylum seekers into alternative accommodation, including former military sites which are designed to be self-contained to reduce impact on the local community.

"As part of the process, we engage with local authorities and police forces to ensure the safety and security of those in the surrounding area."

articles.title: Norfolk police commissioner considers cancelling theatre tour
articles.summary: Colin Sutton is due to perform his true crime show on-stage 127 times between January and November.
articles.body:
Norfolk's police commissioner is considering scrapping his 127-date theatre show after a backlash from local people, he has told the BBC.

Since announcing his UK-wide true crime tour , Colin Sutton said constituents had emailed him with concerns about his ability to perform his day job.

He was elected to the £79,000-a-year post on a Reform UK ticket in July and announced the gig two months later.

Steffan Aquarone, the Liberal Democrat MP for North Norfolk, accused Sutton of acting more like pop star Taylor Swift than a politician.

Police and crime commissioners (PCCs) are elected officials who set the priorities of a police force, appoint a chief constable and hold them to account.

Sutton, who led the investigation to catch serial killer Levi Bellfield , has priced tickets for his "Makings of a Murderer" show at about £40.

The PCC said the theatre tour was not something he needed to mention to voters during the election campaign and he denied letting them down.

Speaking to Chris Goreham on BBC Radio Norfolk, Sutton said the idea for the tour was proposed in 2025, however, he did not commit to the plan and asked promoters to "hold fire" when the PCC by-election happened.

He said: "At the time I was being elected I had said I wasn't going to do it unless I was confident....that it would not be incompatible with doing the job."

Sutton added that since then, the promoters announced a number of tour dates. However he said the tour will now not go ahead in the format that has been published and he is talking with the promoter as to whether or not it should be cancelled entirely.

One of the solutions he proposed was stripping the tour back to venues only local to Norfolk.

He said: "My first priority is this role and to those people who live in Norfolk and I want to come out of my tenure being able to say I made a difference and made things better for them."

He said within the first two months of the role there had been "a lot more work" including long hours, evenings and weekend working that he had not expected .

Sutton is due to appear at a Norfolk police and crime panel on 2 February, before being on stage in Leeds that evening.

"There are lots of people who do meetings like that by [Microsoft] Teams or across the internet now, which might be an option," the ex-detective said.

"But it may well be that it's a moot point now, because I've listened and I think I should make sure the people of Norfolk still have the confidence that I would do the job properly."

Sutton admitted the reaction from constituents on social media and via emails sent to his office had caught him off-guard.

"That's made me think about it again," he conceded.

The role of PCCs in England and Wales is due to be scrapped by the government by the end of Parliament, with their powers to be transferred to newly directly elected mayors.

Aquarone said Sutton had taken the voters of Norfolk for granted by not telling them about the tour.

"Either the job is serious and requires somebody full time paying attention, or it's not and it's OK to go off and do nearly as many tour dates as Taylor Swift," he said.

A spokesperson for Reform said the party was supportive of "celebrity detective" Sutton and pointed out half of his shows would take place at weekends.

articles.summary: US News: Indian-origin woman and her friend, both 24-year-old, from New Jersey were fatally struck by a New York City subway train early Sunday after they were.
articles.body: Indian-origin woman and her friend, both 24-year-old, from New Jersey were fatally struck by a New York City subway train early Sunday after they were seen sitting on the tracks at a Manhattan station. Investigators are trying to determine how and why they ended up in the path of the approaching train.Malaika Chitre and Navam Kaul, both recent Rutgers University graduates, were on the tracks at Spring Street station in Lower Manhattan shortly after 3 am when a southbound No 4 train entered the station. The train operator saw the pair and tried to stop, but was unable to prevent the collision. Both were pronounced dead at the scene. Around 100 passengers were later evacuated from the train, according to reports.The circumstances surrounding the deaths remain unclear. Investigators are examining whether Kaul first fell or went onto the tracks and Chitre followed in an attempt to help him, whether intoxication played a role, or whether the possibility of suicide should be considered.What happened on the tracks?An incident report obtained by the New York Daily News said the train operator told supervisors that she saw the man and woman sitting on the tracks as the train approached. She attempted to stop the train, but it was too late.The report said Chitre appeared to be laughing and pulling Kaul towards her when the train struck them. Separately, law-enforcement sources told the New York Post that Kaul may have fallen or made his way onto the tracks before Chitre went down after him.Video circulating on social media also appeared to show the pair sitting together on the tracks shortly before the train arrived. AmNewYork reported that the operator activated the emergency brake but could not stop the train in time.The medical examiner has not yet released an official determination explaining the circumstances of the deaths.Why were they on the tracks?One possibility being examined is that Kaul ended up on the tracks first and Chitre went down to help him.Police sources told the New York Post that it was not immediately clear whether Kaul had fallen or climbed down. Chitre appeared to try to pull him towards her before the train hit them.If that account is confirmed, Chitre may have gone onto the tracks in an attempt to rescue her friend, rather than intentionally placing herself in the path of the train.However, investigators have not established what happened immediately before the pair were seen on the tracks.Investigators are also looking into whether one or both of them were intoxicated and may have been too impaired or disoriented to recognise the danger posed by the approaching train, according to law-enforcement sources.The footage showing the pair apparently remaining on the tracks as the train approached has raised questions about whether they understood what was happening around them. But there has been no official finding that alcohol or drugs were involved, and toxicology results, if any, have not been made public.Suicide has also been posed as a possible explanation.No suicide note was found at the scene, according to sources cited by the New York Post. However, the absence of a note does not by itself establish how the pair came to be on the tracks, and investigators have not concluded that their deaths were intentional.At present, there is no publicly established motive for why the two were on the tracks.Who were Malaika Chitre and Navam Kaul?Chitre and Kaul were longtime friends who attended Rutgers University around the same time and graduated in 2024.Chitre, from the Dayton section of South Brunswick, New Jersey, graduated from Rutgers with a degree in public health and a minor in business administration. She was working as a quality operations specialist at pharmaceutical company Acadia Pharmaceuticals and had recently begun pursuing a Doctor of Pharmacy degree at Temple University.Kaul, from Sayreville, New Jersey, graduated from Rutgers Business School with a degree in finance. He had been working as a financial data analyst at Bloomberg since 2025.The two were part of the same social circles and South Asian community around Rutgers, according to people who knew them. Rajnikant Pipalia, whose son was a close friend of Kaul, told the New York Post that the pair had grown up in the same social world and remained part of the same wider group of friends.Their deaths came as they were beginning their professional lives.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Wasp spiders increasingly seen in West Midlands
articles.summary: The large, stripey species is making its way northwards from southern England.
articles.body:
One of the UK's largest spider species has been spotted in the West Midlands as warmer temperatures push it more than 100 miles from its usual habitat.

The wasp spider, known for its distinctive yellow, black and white stripes, is traditionally found in southern England but has been recorded increasingly further north in recent years

Unlike its namesake, the species cannot fly, but spiderlings can travel long distances by "ballooning" on silk strands carried by the wind.

The spider has recently been recorded in Worcestershire, alongside sightings in Herefordshire and Warwickshire, according to Worcestershire Wildlife Trust.

Wendy Carter from the trust said people should not be alarmed by the spider's size.

"I know they're quite scary because they're quite big, but they're phenomenal creatures and they're not going to do us any harm," she said.

Carter and her partner recorded a sighting near Eckington last weekend, adding to a string of reports from across the county.

The spider has also been spotted in Evesham, Broadway and Worcester, with the most recent sighting coming in Feckenham.

"We knew they were in the county because we'd had one record last year and sightings on our borders for a little while," Carter said.

"Then about nine or 10 sightings were reported, all in the south-east of the county along the River Avon.

"So I thought I'd go along the River Avon and find another one."

According to the British Arachnological Society , the bodies of female wasp spiders can grow to about 2cm in length, while males are typically much smaller at about 0.5cm.

They are most commonly found among long grass, thistles and other tall vegetation.

The species was first recorded in Britain in 1922, when one was caught at Rye in East Sussex, but has expanded rapidly northwards in recent decades.

Carter said warmer temperatures and milder winters were likely helping the spider establish itself in new areas.

"It's also pushing our wildlife further north, so we're losing species that are unable to cope with the warmth and the mildness," she said.

"This is a natural progression. Wasp spiders are one of a long line of species that we're starting to see move into the county from the south of England."

The spiders require at least three months of warm weather and a mild winter to breed successfully.

Female wasp spiders are currently laying egg sacs before dying off as temperatures fall later in the year.

Despite their intimidating appearance, Carter said they posed no threat to humans.

"All spiders are venomous because that's how they catch their prey," she said, but added: "Only a handful can pierce human skin and none have venom that can harm us."

Anyone who spots a wasp spider in Worcestershire is encouraged to take a photograph and alert Worcestershire Wildlife Trust.

articles.summary: India News: PRAYAGRAJ: Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath on Monday took a swipe at the previous Samajwadi Party government, saying that before 2017, th.
articles.body: PRAYAGRAJ: Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath on Monday took a swipe at the previous Samajwadi Party government, saying that before 2017, the state faced not only a shortage of resources but also issues related to governance, transparency, accountability, law and order, and judicial infrastructure.Additionally, the chief minister revealed plans to provide tablets to 400 state law officers to equip them with modern technology, enabling them to access information on government-related cases before the courts.In another announcement, Adityanath said the state government would introduce a cashless insurance scheme providing coverage of up to Rs 5 lakh for practising advocates in Uttar Pradesh.Addressing a felicitation ceremony organised by the Allahabad High Court Bar Association here, Adityanath said nearly 45 to 50 per cent posts in the Uttar Pradesh Police were vacant before his government assumed office in 2017."Before 2017, the challenge before us was not merely of resources. It was also a challenge of the system and approach, transparency and accountability in administration, law and order and judicial infrastructure," the chief minister said.He highlighted that the police force's annual training capacity at that time was only about 3,000 personnel but has now increased to 60,000."There was no training capacity and even basic facilities for the police were lacking," Adityanath said, adding that his government has strengthened police infrastructure and training facilities across the state.Adityanath also addressed the condition of the subordinate judiciary before 2017, pointing out that many courts operated in dilapidated or temporary buildings, and that district courts in as many as ten districts functioned from rented premises.Furthermore, he stated that his government had also addressed several shortcomings that earlier hampered the criminal justice system, including witnesses turning hostile out of fear in serious criminal cases and inadequate arrangements for transporting prisoners from jails to courts."Today, you can see the results of better coordination between the executive and the judiciary. When we reform and transform, the performance becomes visible on its own," the chief minister said.He emphasised that a robust judiciary strengthens the foundations of good governance, which should be the top priority of any elected government.Adityanath noted hat his government has prioritised greater use of technology, modernised infrastructure, and improved coordination between police and prosecution, leading to significant increases in conviction rates.He pointed out that the prosecution system is now connected to online platforms to ensure timely charge sheet filings and effective presentations of scientific evidence in court.Referring to emerging challenges, Adityanath said the legal fraternity must prepare itself for areas ranging from cybercrime and artificial intelligence to data privacy, e-commerce, fintech, intellectual property and climate litigation."A future-ready Bar will lay a strong foundation for a future-ready justice system," he said, adding that the younger generation of lawyers has a major responsibility in carrying forward the rich traditions of the Allahabad High Court.The chief minister said that district courts and jails have been provided with high-speed internet and video conferencing facilities. Additionally, the virtual recording of evidence and the digitization of court documents are being promoted to reduce trial delays."Justice delayed is justice denied," he said, stressing that timely and impartial justice was essential to maintaining public faith in the judiciary and other democratic institutions.Integrated court complexes were being developed to provide judicial facilities, residential accommodation for judicial officers, chambers for lawyers and other amenities under one roof, he said.Moreover, he outlined welfare measures for advocates, announcing that financial assistance from the lawyers' welfare fund has increased from Rs 1.5 lakh to Rs 5 lakh. The age limit for financial assistance to the families of deceased advocates has also been raised from 60 to 70 years.Adityanath said a strong judiciary forms the foundation of good governance and called for continued coordination and mutual respect between the Bar and the Bench."Only a future-ready Bar can lay a strong foundation for a future-ready justice system," he said.Adityanath announced that the state government would fully support the provision of essential facilities, including furniture and equipment, for the chambers constructed for over 10,000 lawyers as part of the multi-level parking and chamber complex.He stated that the government would assist in receiving proposals through the judiciary and the chief justice. articles.title: AI 'SpongeBob' parody of problems in Egypt draws scrutiny of authorities
articles.summary: A take on the hit US TV series has become an unlikely tool for Egyptians to complain about life amid strict surveillance.
articles.body:
An AI-generated version of the hit US cartoon character SpongeBob SquarePants has recently become the unlikely star of a controversial online trend by Egyptians criticising living conditions, amid strict rules about political dissent.

A wave of satirical postings began last month with a Facebook group dedicated to "Complaints of the Residents of al-Hamour Bottom" - the Arabic name used for SpongeBob's underwater home, Bikini Bottom.

Soon images were showing Egypt's President, Abdul Fattah al-Sisi, as the money-grabbing Mr Krabs, a seabed overcrowded by tuk-tuks (automated rickshaws), and schoolgirl fish being sexually harassed by sleazy, male fish.

Other posts prompted comments complaining about allegedly corrupt ministers, skyrocketing rent, and the poor state of health and education.

The manipulated images of the SpongeBob programme, originally produced by Nickelodeon, were created by users of the site.

Within a couple of weeks, the Facebook group had picked up 1.8m followers. One astute cartoon depicted ministry of interior staff underwater, warning: "Be careful", before the group was suspended, amid reports of official scrutiny.

A teenage girl who claimed she was the group's administrator put a video clip online saying that she and her fellow creators should not be held responsible for political posts that some members had posted in spin-off groups.

Pro-government media and TV presenters accused the outlawed Islamist Muslim Brotherhood, of exploiting the viral phenomenon. Egypt's military ousted the Brotherhood-backed President Mohammed Morsi in 2013, following mass protests against his one-year rule.

"The trend of al-Hamour Bottom belongs to the Brotherhood," insisted well-known talk show host Tamer Abdel Monaim in a programme dedicated to the topic. "Its aim is to sow confusion."

While many posts containing the most sensitive political comments have now been removed, some of the most popular content has continued to circulate widely on social media. Many Egyptian celebrities, social media influencers and brands adopted the theme, sharing AI-generated memes of al-Hamour Bottom.

"The laughter surrounding Bikini Bottom is not necessarily a sign of happiness," the Egyptian radio presenter Rabab Kamal told her thousands of Facebook followers. "People are laughing because circumstances have become so absurd that laughter feels like the only possible response."

Home to more than 110m people, Egypt is the most populated Arab country. Since the 2011 Arab Spring, it has been through years of social and economic upheaval. Ordinary Egyptians still struggle with high inflation from previous currency devaluations affecting their standard of living.

Regional instability has hit Suez Canal revenues, tourism and remittances from Egyptians working in the Gulf. Fuel costs have risen and this summer, the government raised some electricity tariffs by 12%.

At the same time, there is increased intolerance for public dissent in Egypt since the military, led by Sisi, returned to power. The government fears instability and challenges to its rule.

The surreal humour of SpongeBob and his aquatic friends - particularly popular with Millennials and Generation Z - became an unlikely way to work around this.

"The Egyptian government has long been cracking down on online expression. Thousands of people in Egypt languish for years in pretrial detention simply for expressing views online that are not sanctioned by the state," says Mahmoud Shalaby, a regional researcher at Amnesty International.

"This repression is not limited to political opponents. It extends to a wide range of people, including religious minorities, people who do not adhere to a religion, people perceived to be LGBTI, and female social media creators who are often prosecuted under vague morality laws."

Although Sisi insists he is committed to freedom of expression and that Egyptians are free to air any views, few are buying it. Late last month, the president appeared to obliquely reference the SpongeBob craze when he referred to "social media chaos" and how ongoing public discussions failed to grasp the magnitude of national challenges.

Egyptian state security encourages reporting on suspicious or anti-government behaviour.

It may not come as any surprise then that already a lawyer has reportedly submitted a legal complaint against "the administrators, operators, financiers and contributors behind the creation of online content, pages and social media accounts associated with al-Hamour Bottom".

The Cairo 24 news site says he has called for a review into "satirically depicting economic conditions and decisions in a manner that could disturb public security and social order".

The mounting pressure means that SpongeBob could soon be setting aside his new pharaonic costume and giving up the pyramids and his Egyptian home.
