articles.title: Palestine weekly: Settlement sanctions spark diplomatic crisis
articles.summary: New B’Tselem report frames events on ground as Israel’s ‘project of elimination’ of Palestinians.
articles.body:
This past week, a flurry of Western countries announced forthcoming sanctions on Israel – limited, for now, to its illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank. Israel’s response was swift and aggressive: on September 9, it gave the United Kingdom 30 days to close its consulate in occupied East Jerusalem.

As Israel hardened its international defiance, such diplomatic moves did little to slow the dispossession of Palestinian land and identity in Jerusalem and the West Bank, as well as the ongoing killings and deterioration of basic conditions in Gaza.

Such efforts can be difficult to grasp as a single, coordinated process. But a newly released B’Tselem report attempts to do exactly that, describing the overarching colonial system as being driven by aspirations of “elimination” – “the sustained undermining of the conditions that allow Palestinians to exist as an independent collective with land, institutions, language, culture, social ties, leadership, shared memory and history and a social and political horizon”.

International sanctions prompt aggressive Israeli response

Twelve countries , including the UK, France and Canada, announced on September 8 that they would introduce, support, or consider restrictions on Israeli settlement goods, with Britain’s Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband telling parliament that the government could no longer “stand by” in the face of what he called “ethnic cleansing of Palestinians… perpetrated by settler terrorists”.

Israel retaliated within 24 hours, ordering the UK consulate’s closure , ending British training of Palestinian Authority security forces, removing British staff from the Gaza coordination centre in Kiryat Gat and barring 12 British public figures – including 11 members of parliament.

Israel’s aggressive targeting of perceived detractors turned within as well, as Israeli Culture Minister Miki Zohar said he would move to revoke the citizenship of filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor. That is after their documentary “NAZA”, which highlights Israel’s use of AI targeting systems in Gaza, won a Special Jury Prize at Venice and received a 25-minute standing ovation. Zohar called the film “vile” and accused its makers of “treason”.

Gaza: a week of attacks amid a health system nearing collapse

Visiting Ireland this week, US President Trump insisted “there’s very little happening right now in Gaza”. Every day this week told a different story: attacks on Palestinians added to the Strip’s ever-increasing death toll and its already widespread destruction, as humanitarian conditions worsened unabated.

Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich said on September 12 that if European countries took in 20,000 to 30,000 Gaza residents each, “this entire issue would be over”. With no such mass ‘emigration’ materialising yet, airstrikes on Gaza continued on a daily basis.

Following two days of multiple air raids on Gaza wounding women and children, on September 10, Israeli warplanes killed a family of four – father, mother and their two daughters – in the Beit Lahia housing project. Israel alleged the father was involved in attacks. This was followed the next day with a drone strike near the Sumoud camp in Khan Younis, killing Jihad Ismail, 33, and wounding 12 others.

On September 12, a pregnant woman, Iman Shalouf, 27, died from wounds sustained days earlier by Israeli gunfire south of Khan Younis. The next day, an air strike on a vehicle in Gaza City’s Tal al-Hawa neighbourhood killed two Palestinians and wounded 13. On September 14, a Palestinian was killed by Israeli gunfire in the al-Mawasi area of Rafah. On the same day, Gaza’s Ministry of Health put the cumulative toll since October 2023 at 73,786 killed and 174,771 wounded, with 1,372 killed since last October’s “ceasefire”.

Meanwhile, Gaza’s health and transport systems edged closer to collapse. Al-Ahli Arab Hospital said its main generator failed because of a lack of oil and spare parts. That suspended its imaging department – including the only functioning CT scanner in northern Gaza. On September 13, Gaza’s public bus operators’ union said it would suspend transport for doctors and nurses beginning on September 16 due to the lack of replacement parts and fuel; the Health Ministry called it “a death sentence” for patient care.

The latest data from the UN’s Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) found that since March, only 13,445 litres of engine oil have been approved by Israel for entry in Gaza against nearly 93,000 pending – oil needed to keep water, sanitation and hospital generators running.

The diplomatic rupture over settlements was matched this week by a convergence of reports from NGOs and international bodies reaching similar conclusions about conditions in the West Bank.

Israeli rights groups Yesh Din, Bimkom and HaMoked concluded in a joint report that land seizures, settler violence and movement restrictions “form a continuous process” amounting to “de facto annexation.” The B’Tselem report describes “the growing role of settler militias operating in coordination and cooperation with official forces”, working towards the same end even when not literally acting together. This week’s daily incidents put those dynamics on display.

On September 12, in Faqua, near Jenin, a soldier was filmed shooting Qassem Hussam in the leg during a settler incursion onto Palestinian land – an incident Israeli army radio itself said was carried out “contrary to orders” against a man who “posed no threat”, as the ongoing pogrom against Palestinians in the West Bank continued.

A similar pattern played out on September 11, when Palestinian field activists reported that settlers beat five men with metal pipes on the Ramallah-Jericho road, fracturing one man’s knee; no soldiers intervened, though the road runs through an area with a heavy army presence.

Elsewhere, it was Israeli forces carrying out the violence. On September 13, Israeli forces shot and wounded two Palestinian labourers in Beit Jala, according to WAFA. On September 14, forces wounded a young man in Beit Ula, near Hebron, while setting his vehicle on fire, and separately arrested men in Beit Ummar and Dura, according to WAFA.

articles.title: A UK farmer started with 20 sheep on 18 acres; free grazing beneath solar panels helped her expand to more than 200 sheep and 250 acres
articles.summary: UK News: For first-generation sheep farmer Hannah Thorogood, gaining access to land beneath solar panels has opened a new chapter in her farming journey. She b.
articles.body: For first-generation sheep farmer Hannah Thorogood, gaining access to land beneath solar panels has opened a new chapter in her farming journey. She began with just 20 sheep on 18 acres in Lincolnshire, a scale she says was all she could afford at the time. Today, her flock has grown to more than 200 sheep, while the land available to her has expanded to 250 acres. Free grazing on solar sites has helped the change, where sheep manage grass beneath the panels. Thorogood says the arrangement has given her a “massive leg-up” in an industry where land can be difficult to secure.How solar grazing helped Hannah expandSolar grazing involves using sheep to manage vegetation growing beneath and around solar panels. Solar farms need grassland to be kept under control, and the Guardian reported that maintaining a typical site can involve tens of acres of grass that would otherwise need mowing or spraying. Those conventional maintenance methods can cost as much as £50,000 a year.Sheep provide an alternative because they can graze in spaces that machinery cannot easily reach. They move between solar panel supports and consume vegetation without heavy mowing equipment. For farmers such as Thorogood, that creates a chance to use land that is already occupied by renewable-energy infrastructure while providing pasture for their animals.Benefits for sheep and landThorogood says the arrangement has brought several benefits for both her flock and the land. She believes the sheep improve soil quality and increase pasture diversity, while their grazing means the land does not need spraying.The panels also provide shelter for the sheep. Thorogood said the land is secure because cameras are present across the site, while technology teams monitor the flock. She added that the solar panels give the animals protection from snow and extreme heat, providing a form of shelter alongside the grazing they offer.Solar grazing offers farmers new opportunitiesAs reported by the Guardian, Thorogood's experience comes as farmers across the UK face high costs and limited access to agricultural land. The country has traditionally been largely self-sufficient in sheep meat, but high feed and farming costs, the market and weak profitability have contributed to falling sheep numbers.Nicola Noble of the National Sheep Association described free grazing on solar sites as a “valuable opportunity for new, younger or smaller farmers”. Dr Liz Genever, another Lincolnshire sheep farmer, told the Guardian that free solar grazing had enabled her to triple her sheep numbers and said that reaching the full potential of a nearby solar site could increase her income from sheep from £20,000 to £60,000.Combining farming with renewable energyThe model has been presented as a way of combining renewable-energy generation with agricultural use of the same land. Emilien Simonot of Lightsource BP described suitable solar grazing as a “triple-win” for farming, renewables and society, while Lancaster University professor Alona Armstrong said that this type of multiple land use is vital.Not every solar site is suitable for sheep, and concerns have been raised about biodiversity and whether grazing is always carried out at appropriate stocking densities. Noble also warned that grazing should not simply become a public-relations exercise for solar developers. For Thorogood, though, free access to solar-site pasture has provided something particularly valuable: a way to expand her sheep enterprise when agricultural land would otherwise have been difficult to afford.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: National Hispanic Heritage Month begins with celebrations across the U.S.
articles.summary: Celebrations across the U.S. are expected in observance of National Hispanic Heritage Month, showcasing the vast diversity and culture of Latinos.
articles.body: Celebrations across the U.S. are expected in observance of National Hispanic Heritage Month, showcasing the vast diversity and culture of Latinos. Marked each year from Sept. 15 to Oct. 15, the month is an opportunity for many in the U.S. to learn about or be reminded of the contributions of Hispanic people. The nation’s largest racial or ethnic minority, over 70 million ethnically Hispanic residents make up one-fifth of the total U.S. population, according to the census. The group includes people whose ancestors come from Spain, Mexico, the Caribbean and Central and South America. Heritage month honors the cultures and legacy of Latinos National Hispanic Heritage Month started as Hispanic Heritage Week. Mexican American U.S. Rep. Edward R. Roybal of Los Angeles created legislation for it and President Lyndon B. Johnson signed it into law in 1968. It wasn’t until two decades later that it expanded into a month under President Ronald Reagan. “It was clustered around big celebrations for the community,” said Alberto Lammers, director of communications at the UCLA Latino Policy and Politics Institute. “It became a chance for people to know Hispanic cultures, for Latinos to get to know a community better.” Sept. 15 was chosen as a tribute to the anniversary of “El Grito de Dolores,” or the “Cry of Dolores,” which was a call to battle issued in 1810 in Mexico’s war for independence from Spain. Several Central American nations including El Salvador and Guatemala also celebrate their independence in September. Labor movement ties into Latino observance The festivities spotlight the interconnected struggles of Latin and Caribbean nations — including Costa Rica, Nicaragua, Guatemala, Honduras and El Salvador — and a history of fighting for the rights of Indigenous people, said Paul Ortiz, a professor of Latina/o labor history at Cornell University. “The centrality of family, mutual aid, and community is very important to us because our parents, our grandparents, we’ve had to struggle to really make it in this country,” said Ortiz, a former president of the United Faculty of Florida AFL-CIO union. Coming from collectivist cultures is partly why Latinos join labor unions at a higher rate, he added. “We understand the importance of collaboration, collective struggle in terms of improving wages and working conditions,” Ortiz said. With the U.S. Latino consumer base growing over the past decade, historians say there’s an expanded curiosity and appreciation for the Latino community, especially during fraught political times. It also may be a time to reflect on the history of colonialism within Latin America. “There are long trajectories of the racialization of people from Latin America in the U.S. but it’s also the same contributions of these people who made the U.S. what it is,” said Diego Javier Luis, a historian and assistant professor at Johns Hopkins University. Hispanic versus Latino label The Hispanic label was created by the federal government for people from Spanish-speaking cultures. But for some, the identifier inherently carries political conservatism and emphasizes a connection to Spain. It sometimes gets mistakenly swapped with “Latino” or “Latinx.” Latino reflects ties to Latin America. So some will celebrate Hispanic Heritage Month as Latinx or Latin Heritage Month. Latin Americans are not a monolith. From Mexican American to Colombian American to Salvadoran American, each culture in the diaspora has unique differences when it comes to food, art and music. “The history of Latinos is U.S. history, Latino cultures are U.S. culture, Latino foods are U.S. foods, and our music is U.S. music,” Luis said. “It’s also about the people holding these communities together — the mothers, midwives, barbers, bodega owners, artists, poets.”

articles.title: In 1900, North American tall goldenrod was introduced to Japan for gardens and honey production, but it escaped cultivation and overran native grasslands nationwide
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Explore how the North American tall goldenrod, originally introduced to Japan for gardening and honey production, has become one of the country's most notorious invasive species, impacting native grasslands and ecosystems.
articles.body: The majority of plants brought in for beekeeping and gardening remain exactly where they are planted; thus, they rarely receive any attention. Occasionally, however, a species that appears innocuous in a flower bed has very different ambitions when it comes to open space. One of the most obvious instances of that pattern in the world is the tall, late-blooming perennial tall goldenrod, which is native to North America. Japan has been observing the effects of this pattern throughout its countryside for more than a century.Japan's National Institute for Environmental Studies records the first introduction of tall goldenrod at around 1900, when it was deliberately brought in as an ornamental plant and nectar source. It was intentionally introduced as an ornamental garden plant and a nectar source for honeybees because it blooms unusually late in the year, from October through December in much of Japan, when few other plants are still flowering.A plant that flourished precisely where no one wanted itIn its first several decades in Japan, tall goldenrod did much of what gardeners expected of it, staying mainly limited to the plots where it was planted. This changed abruptly in the years after the Second World War, when the plant grew swiftly throughout the country, going well out of gardens into riverbanks, vacant lots, the boundaries of farmland and roadsides. Today, it is established across almost the entire Japanese archipelago.Its success is partly a matter of raw biology. According to the CABI Compendium, tall goldenrod is an international scientific reference maintained by the nonprofit research organisation CABI. Tall goldenrod produces huge numbers of wind-dispersed seeds and also spreads aggressively through underground rhizomes, allowing a single colonising plant to expand into a dense stand within a few growing seasons. It also exudes allelopathic molecules from its roots, chemicals that restrict the germination and growth of competing plants nearby. This gives tall goldenrod an edge over the natural flora in the same patch of soil. Studies comparing Japanese populations with those in the native range have found that the invasive plants tend to grow taller, produce more leaves and release higher concentrations of suppressive compounds, suggesting they have become more aggressive since arriving in Japan.Choking out the grasses that get in firstJapan’s natural grassland populations have mostly borne the ecological penalty. Once established, tall goldenrod forms dense stands that crowd out native grasses and wildflowers that would otherwise share the open ground. The National Institute for Environmental Studies mentions competition with native species and allelopathic suppression as the two known effects of the plant, with native grasses specifically identified among the affected plant. The institute classifies tall goldenrod as one of the 100 worst invasive alien species in Japan, a list of introduced organisms that are considered to cause substantial and enduring damage to the country’s ecosystems.Tall goldenrod remains widespread in Japan, despite its classification as one of the country's 100 worst invasive alien species. NIES lists competition with native species and allelopathic effects among its impacts and notes that pulling and repeated mowing can be used to control established plants. Part of the rationale comes from the very stuff that made the plant desirable in the first place. Its late-season blooms continue to provide a key source of nectar for honeybees and other pollinating insects as they enter the winter months, and wholesale removal from a landscape can leave those insects with fewer options at a time of year when alternatives are already few. They have a dilemma, an unwelcome invader battling a plant that some elements of the ecology and the beekeeping industry have discreetly grown to depend on.A plant still adapting to JapanScientists examining tall goldenrod in Japan have revealed that the populations there are not just frozen copies of those in North America. A reciprocal transplant study summarised by the National Center for Biotechnology Information found evolutionary differences between the two regions, including changes in the resistance of Japanese populations to local insect pests compared with plants in their native range. For example, a species of lace bug that arrived in Japan from the United States fairly recently reacts differently to the goldenrod's resistance mechanisms there than it does to the same plant species back home, a sign that a century and a quarter of separation has already started to alter the way the species defends itself. More than a century after tall goldenrod was brought to a few Japanese gardens for its late flowers and its value to bees, it is one of the most obvious examples in the country of how a plant chosen for one thing can do something else altogether when left to its own devices in unfamiliar soil.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1907, New Jersey's Clementon Park opened; after surviving a 1931 fire and a $2.37 million foreclosure rescue in 2021, it has permanently closed; now the 52-acre site goes on sale
articles.summary: US News: After more than a century of welcoming families through its gates, Clementon Park and Splash World in Camden County, New Jersey, has announced the ‘di.
articles.body: After more than a century of welcoming families through its gates, Clementon Park and Splash World in Camden County, New Jersey, has announced the ‘difficult decision’ to close permanently. The landmark amusement park made the announcement on September 9, marking an end to its 119 years of operation. The property is now up for sale.The end of a 119-year rideOne of New Jersey’s oldest amusement parks, Clementon Park and Splash World, located in Camden County, had operated continuously since 1907, when Theodore Gibbs and his sons opened it as a trolley park. Over the years, it has welcomed millions of visitors, survived the fire in 1931, weathered ownership changes, and, more recently, even navigated the financial turbulence that has claimed many regional parks over the past decade.On September 9, the park said the 2026 season would be its last. The announcement came two days after the park’s final day of operations for the year wrapped up. In a statement, the park authorities said that they were closing permanently and that the park was up for sale. “We are saddened to announce that we have made the difficult decision to close the park and plan to offer the park for sale.”They added, “It has been a privilege to care for a place that has meant so much to generations of families. We are hopeful that we will find a buyer who shares our love for Clementon Park and will carry its history and legacy forward,” the park said in a statement shared on its website. “As we close out our 2026 season, we want to sincerely thank our guests, Season Passholders, team members, and community for being part of another summer at Clementon Park & Splash World.”They said more details regarding the sale would be shared ‘as they become available’. “Thank you for the memories, the support and five wonderful seasons. We are truly grateful to everyone who has been part of this journey,” they added.IB Parks & Entertainment, the Chicago-based company that has owned the property for five years, didn’t specify any reason for the closure. The company acquired the 52-acre site in 2021 through a foreclosure auction for $2.37 million, just two years after the park had temporarily shut down due to the previous owner’s loan defaults. A brief reopening in June 2021 gave the park another run; however, lower attendance and operating pressures affected the park.A rare survivorClementon Park & Splash World is one of the oldest operating amusement parks in the world. The park first opened in 1907, when Theodore Gibbs and his two sons introduced it as a traditional ‘trolley park’, built at the end of a transit line. The growing popularity of trolley lines drew visitors from neighbouring Camden. In 1931, a fire nearly destroyed the park, but it survived. The Gibbs family’s original stewardship lasted until 1977, before ownership passed to others. For decades afterwards, the park changed hands repeatedly. In 1993, it underwent a renovation, adding the Splash World waterpark, featuring multiple water slides, a wave pool, a lazy river, and the 13,000-square-foot Aquatic Paradise ‘sprayground’. The renovation cost $5 million, and it also attracted more visitors.Then came the 2019 crisis, when loan defaults left the park dark. The 2021 purchase by IB Parks & Entertainment was a rescue. As the company operates multiple parks across the country, including Indiana Beach and Sahara Sam’s, this rescue gave hope that Clementon might integrate into a larger portfolio.But five years proved insufficient. IB Parks & Entertainment has faced challenges across its holdings. Its New York property, Niagara Amusement Park & Splash World on Grand Island, did not open for the 2026 season, citing attendance and revenue shortfalls.What’s next for the park? The company has offered the property for sale, hoping to find a buyer willing to preserve the park’s legacy. If such a buyer emerges, New Jerseyans may still have a place that holds memories of a century. Whether that’s realistic remains uncertain. Regional parks usually depend on real estate value or development potential as much as operating margins. A 52-acre property in Camden County may appeal more to developers than to potential operators. The future of the park now hangs on its next buyer.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Why Alia Bhatt has been sending emails to daughter Raha since her birth: “When she's 15, I'd give this to her and say…”
articles.summary: For many parents, a child’s early years pass in a blur of photographs, videos and small moments that are easy to forget. Alia Bhatt has found her own .
articles.body: For many parents, a child’s early years pass in a blur of photographs, videos and small moments that are easy to forget. Alia Bhatt has found her own way of keeping those memories together. The actor has been sending emails to her daughter Raha every month since her birth, collecting photographs, videos and personal thoughts that she hopes to share with her when she is older.In a conversation with author and podcaster Jay Shetty, Alia explained why she chose emails instead of a traditional memory book. She also spoke about watching her daughter grow up, the memories she is collecting with her family and how becoming a mother has changed the way she sees her own parents.“I’m doing this thing where I send Raha emails”Alia said she started sending emails to Raha soon after her birth and has continued doing so every month. “I’m doing this thing where I send Raha emails. I’ve been doing it every month since she’s born. Just like an amalgamation of photos and videos and what happened and just thoughts and feelings,” she said.The idea came to her after somebody suggested it. Rather than writing in a physical diary, Alia chose a digital format that she could update regularly. “Yeah, somebody said this to somebody, so I was like, it’s a great idea because it’s like a live memory book, you know? I don’t have the discipline and the energy to actually fill out a physical memory book, so I thought this is like a digital way of doing it. It’s easier to search, and it’s nice because maybe when she’s 15, you know, I’d give this to her and say, ‘Listen, this is all the memories that we collected for you over the years. Go ahead and have some fun,’” she told Jay.What does Alia put in the emails?When Jay asked what she had collected so far, Alia said the emails mostly contain visuals and small notes about Raha’s life. “Just photos, you know, videos, thoughts, mainly just visuals of her with either us, with either one of us, or her grandparents, or her aunt or uncle and stuff like that,” she said. She explained that the collection includes random moments rather than a carefully planned record.“Just random moments, you know, and like a little note that you did this today, and we had such a lovely trip here, and something happened, and just sharing whatever I can. It’s like within the moments, whatever comes out at that time,” Alia said.“When she’s 15, I’d give this to her”The actor has a particular age in mind for sharing the collection with her daughter. Alia said she might give the emails to Raha when she turns 15, allowing her to look through the memories gathered since birth. “Maybe when she’s 15, you know, I’d give this to her and say, ‘Listen, this is all the memories that we collected for you over the years. Go ahead and have some fun,’” she said.Alia also spoke about recording moments involving her daughter and family members. “But yeah, so when I’m sneakily recording the two of them, sometimes when I review it, it’s really very heartwarming to watch because you know that this is like something very special is just cooking,” she said.A memory from New York and a conversation about parentsDuring the conversation, Alia recalled a memory involving her mother and a photograph of a baby. “I remember in New York we were speaking about this, and I remember my mom sent me a photo of a baby walking down the street with many bags. It was like a random Pinterest image or something,” she said.The image led Alia and her mother to reflect on how parents continue to see their children as babies, even after they grow up. “And we actually both agreed that we’re actually all giant babies through our lives, at least for our parents. Like no matter how old we become, we’re still babies,” Alia said.She connected the thought to her own experience as a daughter and a mother. “And I see that now. I see that now when every time I would travel, my mom would say, ‘Okay, be careful before you cross the road. Take care of your arms and legs.’ yeah, I’m like, ‘What do you say? What do you mean, take care of your arms and legs?’ But I understand that now,” she said.Looking for trusted parenting advice? articles.title: A 66-million-year-old gastropod fossil was found at a 5,000-year-old settlement in Ankara; ancient inhabitants may have brought it there
articles.summary: Rest of World News: A 66-million-year-old gastropod fossil has been discovered at an archaeological site in Ankara, Turkey. Excavators uncovered the fossil during work at.
articles.body: A 66-million-year-old gastropod fossil has been discovered at an archaeological site in Ankara, Turkey. Excavators uncovered the fossil during work at Kulhoyuk in the Oyaca neighbourhood of Ankara’s Golbasi district. Researchers believe it dates to one of the final phases of the Tethys Sea, an ancient body of water that once covered parts of Central Anatolia. The creature existed millions of years before the settlement was established about 5,000 years ago. According to the Anadolu Agency of Turkey, the specimen may have been found elsewhere and later brought to Kulhoyuk by the settlement’s ancient inhabitants.What was the 66-million-year-old fossil found in AnkaraThe fossil belongs to a gastropod, a group of mollusks that includes snails and slugs. It was discovered during archaeological excavations at Kulhoyuk, in Ankara’s Golbasi district. Researchers believe the specimen dates to one of the final phases of the Tethys Sea. The ancient sea began forming about 250 million years ago and once covered parts of Central Anatolia. The fossil therefore predates the settlement by millions of years. The discovery connects Kulhoyuk’s archaeological history with a much older geological past and gives researchers another clue about the site’s history.What makes the fossil’s presence at Kulhoyuk rareThe fossil, however, is about 66 million years old, long before people lived at Kulhoyuk. The gastropod therefore belonged to a much earlier period than the settlement’s inhabitants. Researchers are considering whether ancient residents may have found the fossil elsewhere before bringing it to Kulhoyuk. This would make the discovery different from a fossil found in the geological setting where it originally formed. It also leaves researchers with questions about how the specimen reached the settlement and why its ancient inhabitants may have chosen to keep it there.Mystery behind the fossil’s presence at KulhoyukResearchers are considering whether people living at Kulhoyuk thousands of years ago found the fossil elsewhere and brought it to the settlement. However, this remains a possibility rather than a confirmed explanation for how it got there. Researchers would need to establish where the fossil came from and why ancient inhabitants may have decided to keep it at the site. Its age adds another layer to the mystery, since the people at Kulhoyuk were handling an object that had formed millions of years before their time. The discovery has opened another area of investigation into how the fossil reached the settlement and what significance it may have held for those who lived there.How is the fossil connected to the ancient Tethys SeaThe fossil is believed to date to one of the final phases of the Tethys Sea, an ancient body of water that began forming about 250 million years ago and once covered parts of Central Anatolia. The gastropod lived along the shores of this sea about 66 million years ago before eventually becoming fossilised. Its discovery at Kulhoyuk therefore connects the archaeological site with a much older landscape shaped by the ancient sea. The finding does not indicate that the settlement existed during that period. Instead, it offers a glimpse into the region’s geological past, long before communities were established at Kulhoyuk.How are discoveries helping researchers understand KulhoyukThe fossil is the latest notable discovery from Kulhoyuk, where archaeological excavations have been underway since 2021. Archaeologists recently found what they described as the earliest-known seed remains of Ankara’s distinctive ‘Sevgi Cicegi’, or Love Flower, inside a 4,000-year-old Hittite vessel. The excavation programme is backed by the Turkish presidency and led by Associate Professor Derya Yilmaz Tekin on behalf of Ankara University and the Culture and Tourism Ministry. The work is continuing to uncover evidence from the site and its long history.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Law enforcement 'key factor' in falling small boats numbers, says NCA
articles.summary: But other factors, including developments in the Middle East, may also be playing a role.
articles.body:
Law enforcement activity has been a "key factor" in reducing the number of small boat Channel crossings, the National Crime Agency (NCA) says.

The number of people arriving in the UK in the first half of 2026 was down 41% on the year before, government figures show.

The NCA said the drop followed a "significant increase in arrests and seizures", although added "fluctuating demand" for crossings, and the French authorities preventing boat launches had also played a role.

However, Mihnea Cuibus, a senior researcher at the University of Oxford University's Migration Observatory, says it is "impossible" to disentangle the effects of government policy and other factors on small boat arrivals.

While recent policy changes appear to have led smugglers and migrants to alter their behaviour, Cuibus says fewer unauthorised arrivals into the EU and developments in key origin countries - such as improved security in Syria - may be partially behind the decline.

"It is hard to know how much restrictive measures contributed to reducing [arrivals] in 2026," he continues.

He said limitations on refugee family reunion and a reduction in the asylum grant rate could also have had an impact.

The Conservatives have previously said the weather played a huge role in the fluctuating numbers of crossings from France and Belgium.

NCA director general of operations Rob Jones said the agency was "devoting more resources to tackling organised immigration crime than ever before".

"However, we are not complacent, and the job is by no means done," he continued.

"We must continue to keep up the pressure on these criminal gangs, as they continue to put lives at risk in the Channel."

The NCA said organised crime groups had been affected by "supply constraints" on vital equipment used in crossings.

More than 1,600 boats or engines have been seized by the authorities since late 2023, it said.

The wholesale cost of these items has gone up as a result, according to an NCA spokesperson.

The NCA said a "number of key suppliers" had also been targeted, including the jailing of Adem Savas who reportedly supplied equipment used in about half of all crossings in 2023.

However, the NCA also admitted the war in the Middle East had also made it harder for criminals to source dinghies.

It added it could not publish its report on small boats in full because it contained sensitive intelligence.

The NCA also pointed to activity targeting people smugglers reducing small boat crossings.

In the year to April 2026, arrests linked to organised immigration crime involving the NCA increased by more than 55%, it said.

The agency added it had also worked with social media networks to have more than 40,000 posts pages or accounts linked to immigration crime removed.

"We are making it more difficult and costlier for people smuggling networks to source equipment, more difficult to get it to the beaches and in the water, more difficult to communicate with potential customers, and more likely smugglers will be confronted by law enforcement," said Jones.

"Our message to the gangs is clear – moving people in small boats and supplying equipment gets riskier for you by the day," he continued.

However, the Migration Observatory said "most notably" there had been a sharp decline in detected unauthorised border crossings into the EU.

It said arrivals fell 26% in 2025, before declining another 37% in the first half of 2026.

"This is likely to lead, with a lag, to fewer unauthorised crossings to the UK, since most small boat migrants travel through the EU before reaching beaches in northern France," it added.

In August, the Home Office credited police in France with intercepting 185 potential crossings involving 4,300 migrants this summer over four separate weeks, as well as stopping 12 boats at sea using new techniques.

Many migrants come from some of the poorest parts of the world and almost all ask to claim asylum once they are picked up by the UK authorities.

Home Office figures show a total of 41,472 migrants crossed the Channel in small boats in 2025.

In 2025, there were 24 confirmed deaths related to Channel crossings, down from 73 the year before, according to the University of Oxford's Migration Observatory.

A total of 162 people died in the Channel between 2018 and 2025, it adds.

articles.title: Netherlands rail disruption due to suspected sabotage, operator says
articles.summary: Trains were cancelled or delayed on Tuesday after objects were found on tracks at multiple locations.
articles.body:
Parts of the Netherlands, including Amsterdam, have been hit by major rail disruption after suspected sabotage to the tracks, the country's railway infrastructure operator has said.

ProRail warned that passengers in the country's centre and north should expect cancellations and delays on Tuesday, while the closure of some level crossings could cause disruption to roads.

Pipes were attached to the tracks in multiple locations, according to local media. In a statement, ProRail said the incident appeared to be "an intentional disruption... caused by human action".

It added that no suspects or motives had been identified, but the national police unit was investigating.

The BBC has contacted police for comment.

The network's website showed that at least 15 disruptions had been recorded across the country on Tuesday, with routes to the main international airport, Schiphol, and Utrecht also affected.

Train operator Nederlandse Spoorwegen said services around Zwolle, Deventer, and Amersfoot had been disrupted.

It added that the disruption was so extensive it was "not possible" to provide a bus replacement service.

A Eurostar train from Amsterdam to Paris was also delayed due to "operational restrictions" at Amsterdam Centraal on Tuesday, although it was not clear if this was linked to wider disruption. The BBC has contacted Eurostar for further information.

ProRail said in a statement: "Materials were found at multiple locations in the track that were deliberately placed there. This causes section malfunctions. Sabotage appears to be involved".

Footage published by Dutch public broadcaster NOS on Tuesday showed police carrying what appeared to be metal pipes - about 1.5 metres (5ft) long - away from railway tracks at Veenendaal in the central Netherlands.

One train in the city of Steenwijk struck one of the objects, ProRail said, but added there were no injuries as a result.

The disruption in the Netherlands came after separate reports in French media suggested a derailment in Normandy on Friday could have been an act of sabotage.

According to prosecutors, a section of rail found on the track may have caused the crash. But France's interior minister Laurent Nunez has urged caution while an investigation is ongoing, saying that authorities are pursuing all leads.

articles.title: NATO jets down drone over Lithuania; Russian frigate fires flares at Danish helicopter
articles.summary: NATO fighter jets shot down a drone that entered Lithuanian airspace overnight, officials said Tuesday, less than a day after NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said that strikes close to the alliance’s territory would drive the trans-Atlantic organization to increase its support for Kyiv.
articles.body: NATO fighter jets shot down a drone that entered Lithuanian airspace overnight, officials said Tuesday, less than a day after NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said that strikes close to the alliance’s territory would drive the trans-Atlantic organization to increase its support for Kyiv. The drone was downed near the village of Pratkūnai in the Kaišiadorys district, about 60 miles west of the country’s capital, Vilnius, and near the Kaunas Reservoir, Lithuania’s National Crisis Management Center said Tuesday. Lithuania’s military said that the incident marked the first time that a drone had been shot down in the country’s airspace. Authorities didn’t comment on the drone’s origin or purpose, saying the incident needed further investigation. Meanwhile, a Russian frigate fired two flares toward a Danish military helicopter in international waters off Denmark on Monday, narrowly missing the aircraft, the Nordic NATO member’s military said. The Baltic Sea region is on high alert after incidents involving gas pipeline outages, airspace violations and drone sightings since Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, all of which have increased tensions between Moscow and the West. The Fennec military helicopter had been on a routine mission to photograph the Russian frigate, the Danish defense command said in a statement late on Monday. One of the flares — pyrotechnics usually used as a warning signal at sea — passed close to the helicopter, the defense command said. The Russian embassy did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The incidents follows a speech by Rutte on Monday at NATO headquarters in Brussels, where he said that strikes “close to NATO territory” showed Russian President Vladimir Putin’s “desperation and also his desire to sow fear and terror.” “Russia is growing increasingly reckless as it continues its terrible war against Ukraine,” Rutte said. He also pledged to bolster the 32-nation alliance’s own defenses along its long eastern border with Russia. The menace of drones has repeatedly loomed over the skies of Lithuania, which shares borders with Belarus, a key ally of Moscow, and the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad. Antanas Matutis, commander of the Lithuanian air force, said that the wreckage had been found, and the drone “likely” was carrying explosives. Vilmantas Vitkauskas, head of the crisis center, told Lithuanian public broadcaster LRT that the drone most likely entered from Belarus. It remained in Lithuanian airspace for about 30 minutes and flew along the outskirts of populated areas before being intercepted, he said. Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said the incident at sea was serious but not surprising, calling it part of a pattern in which an increasingly aggressive Russia has intensified its hybrid warfare against Europe and is testing NATO. “Russia wants to sow fear and discord. Our answer is to stand closer together and strengthen the defence of Denmark and Europe,” she said in a statement. Hybrid attacks are typically classified as incidents of aggression that fall short of acts of war. Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen called the incident “unacceptable” and said it could have endangered human lives. “Denmark is working to ensure that all shipping can pass peacefully through Danish waters, but Russia is gradually moving the line for what it considers acceptable behaviour,” he said in a statement. He said he had summoned Russia’s ambassador to Denmark for a meeting. The Danish straits are the main sea route in and out of the Baltic Sea for commercial and military shipping. They are also a major artery for global oil shipments, including from Russia’s so-called shadow fleet of tankers used to circumvent Western sanctions. Denmark‘s Defence Intelligence Service said last year that Russian warships had repeatedly sailed on collision courses with Danish vessels, targeted Danish helicopters and ships with tracking radars, and pointed weapons at them in the straits. Russia has dismissed accusations over such incidents and repeatedly denied carrying out hybrid attacks in Europe.

articles.title: A Wisconsin family tried for years to drain nearly 2,000 floodplain acres for farming; after the effort struggled and a tax fight followed, the land is now permanently protected along 2+ miles of the Sugar River
articles.summary: US News: A Wisconsin family spent years trying to make nearly 2,000 low-lying acres along the Sugar River work as farmland. But the property’s location in a fl.
articles.body: A Wisconsin family spent years trying to make nearly 2,000 low-lying acres along the Sugar River work as farmland. But the property’s location in a floodplain made farming difficult, and the drainage system could not keep pace with the water.The former Applegate-Bader Farm is now permanently protected after Groundswell Conservancy and Ducks Unlimited completed the purchase of the property, The Good Press reported. The land stretches along more than two miles of the Sugar River in Rock County, about 45 minutes south of Madison. It includes wetlands, floodplain forests, prairies and river frontage.The conservation deal came after years of difficulty for the family. In 2016, Applegate-Bader sued Wisconsin’s Department of Revenue after a rule change excluded permanent conservation easements from the state’s “use-value” farmland tax assessment. The dispute went through the courts before the family eventually found a conservation buyer for the property.The purchase is the largest land protection project in Groundswell Conservancy’s 43-year history. It is also Ducks Unlimited’s largest acquisition in Wisconsin. The organisations plan to transfer ownership of the property to the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources, keeping the land protected and open to the public.From farmland to wildlife corridorThe nearly 2,000-acre property will become part of the Avon Bottoms Wildlife Area. The area is already recognised as a state Conservation Opportunity Area and an Important Bird Area. The newly protected land connects wetlands, prairie and forest into one continuous wildlife corridor.“Protecting nearly 2,000 acres at once creates an even larger, connected corridor where wildlife of all kinds can move, feed, nest and thrive,” said Amy Mertz, Groundswell Conservancy’s director of development and communications, as quoted by The Good Press.The property provides habitat for several species, including endangered Yellow-crowned Night-Herons and Ornate Box Turtles. It also supports threatened Cerulean Warblers and Acadian Flycatchers, as well as protected Blanding’s Turtles, according to wildlife biologist Jason Cotter, who spoke to The Daily Cardinal.The wetlands also have a role beyond providing habitat. They filter nutrients, store floodwater and recharge aquifers. The conservation groups said the property is especially significant because large opportunities to protect land of this size are uncommon in southern Wisconsin.Land opens up for public useThe property is already open to the public for hiking, fishing, hunting and wildlife watching. It also provides new access to the lower Sugar River on its south side.Tony Abate, senior director of conservation at Groundswell Conservancy, said the property gives people more space for outdoor activities.“This project creates new access to the lower Sugar River on the south side,” Abate said. “There’s tremendous opportunity for outdoor recreation, so people who love to get outside and hike, birdwatch, hunting, fishing, trapping, cross-country skiing, those kinds of activities. They now have nearly 2,000 more acres to do that.”Abate said the land could have had a different future without the conservation purchase. He said it might have been subdivided and sold to people seeking private recreation, which would have kept the land in private hands and limited public access to the southern part of the lower Sugar River.Habitat work plannedDucks Unlimited plans to manage the property to improve its wildlife habitat. The organisation expects to carry out wetland enhancements and upland management.“We hope to maximize wildlife habitat potential on the property through wetland enhancements and upland management,” said Brian Glenzinski, Ducks Unlimited’s director of conservation programmes for the Upper Midwest.He said one part of the plan will involve controlling woody growth that has spread across the property. Prescribed fire will be used to remove some of that growth and improve nesting habitat for waterfowl and other grassland birds.The land is part of a wider conservation effort around the Avon Bottoms. With this acquisition, the total protected area across four linked Avon Bottoms projects has reached about 2,600 acres.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Decision to reopen Bradford tip with culture cash to be examined
articles.summary: Labour councillor 'calls in' Reform executive's move to use £400,000 to reopen Bradford waste site.
articles.body:
A decision to divert £400,000 of culture funding in Bradford to reopen a tip in the district is to be re-examined by a cross-party panel of councillors.

Earlier this month, Bradford Council's Reform-led cabinet voted to reopen the Sugden End tip in Cross Roads, near Keighley, by the end of the year.

The decision was welcomed by many local residents and politicians, but concerns were raised over how the executive planned to pay for it, and the impact of cutting arts funding to do so.

The executive's decision has now been "called in" by Bingley Labour councillor Susan Fricker, and it will be discussed by a scrutiny committee next Tuesday.

The move will give councillors from all parties a chance to debate the plans before either deciding to accept and "release" the decision - or send it back to the executive to be reconsidered.

Rather than the reopening of the tip, Fricker's reasoning for the call-in relates to the scrapping of culture funding, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service .

The £400,000 was previously included in a budget that was voted through ahead of May's local elections, before Labour lost control of the council.

The money was set aside to "support the delivery of events across the district to promote local heritage, culture and arts and drive increased footfall in district centres".

Fricker pointed out in her official call-in request that £200,000 of that cash pot had been set aside for events, and "bringing people together to celebrate where they live".

The other £200,000 was for "strategic support for local organisations running events".

Her request adds: "The funds were designed for communities to run local events, to support increases in footfall to high streets and town centres, to support local businesses, our creative industries and to enhance local pride in place.

"The termination of these funds will have detrimental impacts upon local communities, local businesses, our creative industries and the reputation of the council."

She said both the executive's report and its recent meeting where the changes were voted through had "failed to give any consideration to the impact of terminating these funds... there was no relevant cost/benefit analysis".

It had also "failed to give any consideration to alternative sources of funding for the HWRC (tip) proposals," she added.

At last week's executive meeting , councillor Imran Khan, leader of the Labour group, said alternative funding should be found to reopen the tip, rather than cutting arts funding.

He said: "It doesn't have to be one or the other."

But council leader Stephen Place said reopening the tip would help the people of Bradford, particularly the Keighley area.

The Reform executive was supported by the opposition Conservative group, with chief whip Geoff Winnard saying scarce resources should be concentrated on "getting the basics right" before spending on "the more frivolous nice-to-have extras".

articles.title: Controversial wind farm plans off Fylde coast approved
articles.summary: The project will see dozens of turbines built more than 20 miles off the Lancashire  coast.
articles.body:
A controversial plan to build high-voltage cables across the Fylde to connect Irish Sea wind farms to the National Grid has been approved by the government despite local opposition.

Fylde Council leader Karen Buckley said the decision "will come as a blow" to residents, community groups and parish councils which have fought the cabling corridor.

The cables will connect the proposed Morgan Offshore Wind Project to the National Grid. Developers said the scheme would see 96 turbines built more than 20 miles (32km) off the Fylde coast and generate enough electricity to power nearly two million homes every year.

Electricity will come ashore on the Lancashire coast before being carried underground to a new grid connection at Penwortham, near Preston.

Under the scheme, cables would come ashore near Starr Gate beach, close to Blackpool Airport, before running through the countryside and into a battery storage facility in Penwortham.

The project also includes substations and other infrastructure, despite objections raised by residents, councils and campaign groups during a public consultation.

Fylde's Conservative MP Andrew Snowden said he was "as stunned as I am angry" that the plans had been approved and said he would work with Fylde Council on next steps.

articles.title: Denmark says Russian warship fired flares at military helicopter
articles.summary: The Danish prime minister has accused Russia of "reckless" behaviour, while the Kremlin is yet to comment.
articles.body:
Denmark has accused a Russian warship of firing two emergency flares at one of its helicopters while it was tracking the vessel in the Baltic Sea.

The Danish government has summoned the Russian ambassador over the incident, which it said happened during a "routine" monitoring operation on Monday.

Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen branded the Russian action "reckless" and said it was designed to "intimidate and divide".

Russia said it would "thoroughly investigate" the incident but accused Danish helicopters of making "dangerous manoeuvres" near Russian warships.

It came on the same day Nato forces shot down a drone over Lithuania in the latest security scare on the alliance's eastern flank, where tensions remain high during Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

In a statement detailing the incident in the Baltic Sea, the Danish armed forces said: "One of the air force's Fennec helicopters was today fired at with flares during a routine photographic operation of a Russian frigate, which was located in international waters off Gedser."

Of the two flares fired at the helicopter, one passed close to it, the statement added.

The Danish foreign ministry described the incident as "completely unacceptable".

Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen accused Russia of "gradually shifting the boundary for what they consider acceptable behaviour", adding: "That is something we cannot accept."

In a statement following the incident, Russian ambassador Vladimir Barbin accused Denmark of "recklessness" and "provocative actions".

Barbin said this was "not the first time that Danish Air Force helicopters have carried out dangerous manoeuvres near Russian warships". He added that the latest incident showed that "communication problems lie not with the Russian Navy's vessels, but with the Danish side".

Danish Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus told Reuters no attempt to make contact with helicopters had been made by the frigate's crew.

Overnight, Nato fighter pilots shot down a drone that entered Lithuania's airspace.

Authorities said the drone likely entered southern Lithuania, near the second-largest city of Kaunas, from neighbouring Belarus shortly after midnight on Tuesday.

The origins of the drone are yet to be determined, the Lithuanian national crisis management centre said, but the country's president pointed to increased Russian aggression in recent months.

President Gitanas Nausėda wrote on X: "With Russia intensifying its aggression against Ukraine, such readiness is vital for our region. Together with our Nato Allies, Lithuania will defend its airspace."

Lithuania shares a large part of its southern and eastern border with Belarus, a key Russian ally.

Poland also announced there had been "aviation operations" in its airspace on Monday night "due to the activity of Russian Federation's jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicles conducting strikes on Ukrainian territory".

It said the overnight operations were of a "preventive nature" and aimed at "securing airspace and its protection, especially in areas adjacent to threatened regions".

Nato jets have been scrambled several times to shoot down stray Ukrainian drones that have crossed into Baltic countries Estonia and Latvia this year.

Ukraine has blamed the stray drones on Russian electronic warfare, technology designed to change the flight paths of Ukrainian drones.

articles.title: Meet Aaryan Shukla, the 16-year-old from Nashik who became the world's number one human calculator with 9 Guinness World Records; His father says, " We are not a family of mental calculators..."
articles.summary: Born on July 6, 2010, in Nashik, Maharashtra, Aaryan Shukla is not your normal teenager. While most 16-year-olds are juggling school assignments and s.
articles.body: Born on July 6, 2010, in Nashik, Maharashtra, Aaryan Shukla is not your normal teenager. While most 16-year-olds are juggling school assignments and screen time, Aaryan has spent the last decade turning mental arithmetic into a genuine sporting career, one that has taken him from a modest household in Nashik to stages in Germany, Italy, Dubai, Russia, and Saudi Arabia. Today, he holds the title of world number one human calculator, backed by nine Guinness World Records and two Mental Calculation World Cup titles. During the conversation with his father, Nitin Shukla, he told us that he is a businessman, while his mother, Meenal Shukla, previously worked in the IT sector before stepping back to support Aaryan's journey full-time. Aaryan studies at Delhi Public School, Nashik, and outside of mental calculation, enjoys cricket, football, and reading, reminders that behind the record-breaking numbers is still a fairly ordinary teenager.From a curious six-year-old to a World Cup champion at 12"Aaryan began practising mental calculation at just six years old," told his father. His early interest quickly stood out, and by the age of eight, he was already representing India internationally, winning ten medals, including seven gold, at the Memoriad Turkey Open Championship in Istanbul in 2018, a haul that remains an unbroken record at that event to this day. The real turning point came in 2022, when Aaryan travelled to Paderborn, Germany, to compete at the Mental Calculation World Cup, an event held once every two years and open only to the top 40 human calculators in the world. At just 12 years old, he became World Champion, competing against and beating adults with years more experience. Two years later, in September 2024, he didn't just defend his title, he dominated it, winning all six trophies on offer and scoring 819.84 points out of a possible 900, while also setting five new world records along the way.Six world records in a single dayPerhaps the most jaw-dropping chapter of Aaryan's career came in December 2024, when Guinness World Records invited him to their official office in Dubai for a dedicated day of record attempts. With only three attempts allowed per category, Aaryan created six new Guinness World Records in a single day, including the fastest time to mentally add 50 five-digit numbers (18.71 seconds) and the fastest time to multiply two five-digit numbers (51.69 seconds). He remains the only person from India to achieve this feat. He had earlier set his first individual Guinness World Record in February 2024 in Milan, Italy, live on the television show Lo Show Dei Record, correctly adding 50 five-digit numbers in his head in just 25.19 seconds.Speaking about his son's rare ability, Nitin Shukla has been candid in interviews with international outlets, including Guinness World Records itself and Sputnik India, insisting that extraordinary calculation skills don't run in the family. "We are a normal family," he has said. "Aaryan is a one in a billion kind of person, but I don't think that we are a family of mental calculators." He has also shared that Aaryan showed an unusual interest in numbers as early as age six and that after just six to eight months of practice, he was already doing things far beyond what an average child his age could manage.A platform that keeps growingAaryan's achievements have opened doors well beyond competition halls. He has appeared on Russia's "The Amazing People" talent show, was invited as guest of honour at the Italian Mental Calculation Championship 2026, spoke at the Misk Global Forum in Riyadh alongside global youth leaders, and even featured at an online session hosted by mathematician Dr Arthur Benjamin for the National Museum of Mathematics in New York. Closer to home, he shared a stage with India's Prime Minister at the CNN-News18 Rising Bharat Summit in 2025 and received financial support from the Maharashtra state government to help fund his international competitions.Why Aaryan's story matters?Aaryan's rise comes at a moment when concerns about basic maths ability among Indian students are hard to ignore. According to the Annual Status of Education Report (ASER) 2022, children's basic maths skills across the country had dropped back to 2018 levels, with declines visible in both government and private schools. Globally too, the latest PISA 2025 assessment found mathematics scores falling across participating countries, continuing a downward trend linked to shorter attention spans and rising digital distraction among students. Against that backdrop, a teenager choosing to spend hours each day training his mind to solve complex calculations without any device feels almost countercultural. Aaryan has spoken about the discipline behind his skill, describing regular practice, focus, and a mindset built around persistence rather than natural genius alone. For a generation growing up reaching instinctively for a calculator app, his journey is a reminder that the human brain, when trained deliberately and consistently, remains remarkably capable.An inspiring reminder for young IndiansWhat makes Aaryan's story resonate isn't simply the trophies or record certificates; it's what his journey represents. A middle-class family in Nashik saw a spark of interest in their six-year-old and chose to nurture it patiently, without any guarantee of where it would lead. A decade later, that patience produced a world champion who has represented India on some of the world's biggest stages, all built on nothing more than consistent practice and self-belief. At a time when concerns about shrinking attention spans and declining number skills are being raised both in India and globally, Aaryan Shukla stands as a rare, tangible example of what focused effort and mental discipline can still achieve, offering today's young generation a genuinely inspiring blueprint: that patience, practice, and a willingness to train the mind itself can still produce something extraordinary.Looking for trusted parenting advice? articles.title: After laying off 3,300 Uber employees, CEO Dara Khosrowshahi says: Customers should see it in what they pay, and in how...
articles.summary: Tech News News: Uber cut about 3,300 jobs earlier this month, close to 10% of its global headcount, and chief executive Dara Khosrowshahi now says riders should event.
articles.body: Uber cut about 3,300 jobs earlier this month, close to 10% of its global headcount, and chief executive Dara Khosrowshahi now says riders should eventually see the result of that decision on their fare screen. Speaking at the Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference last week, he said the money freed up by the restructuring is going straight back into the business, and that cheaper rides sit near the top of that list.The cuts were Uber's largest since the pandemic, and they were not presented as a rescue operation. Khosrowshahi has described the company as growing, profitable and held back mainly by its own org chart. What the layoffs buy, in his telling, is speed and spending room at a moment when robotaxi rivals are moving into cities Uber treats as home turf.Uber layoffs: where the savings are actually goingHe was fairly specific about the destination. The savings go back into the business through "lowering prices, improving selection" and continued spending on growth programmes, he said.Insurance is the second lever. Uber's US mobility insurance costs rose by more than 50% per ride over a few years through the first quarter of 2025, running well ahead of inflation. That curve has since reversed, and part of what the company is no longer paying out is being routed into fares.There is a cross-subsidy at work too, which Khosrowshahi calls a barbell strategy. Margins from premium products such as Uber Black help fund the cheap end of the menu, including Wait & Save, which cuts the fare for riders willing to hang on a few extra minutes for a pickup.Fewer managers, fewer remote roles, a flatter UberThe reorganisation went deeper than headcount. Uber reduced the number of employees sitting seven or more layers below the CEO by 20% and cut micro-teams of one or two reports by nearly half. Core Services engineering and science teams are being merged, and the three delivery operations arms covering restaurants, retail and direct are folding into single units at global, regional and country level.Remote work is effectively over at the company. Going forward only about 1% of staff will work remotely, with the rest expected in an office three days a week under the existing hybrid policy.Waymo pressure is the real reason behind Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi's price talkThe timing explains a lot. Uber's stock is down roughly 12.5% so far this year, even after climbing on the layoff announcement, and analysts have flagged autonomous vehicles as the medium-term threat to its rides business. Uber has an exclusive Waymo partnership in Austin and Atlanta, but Waymo told the company in July that it will begin selling rides through its own app alongside Uber from 2028. Waymo has since launched autonomous rideshare in Nashville with Lyft.Uber is not the only company thinning out this month either. More than 5,000 people across 13 companies have been laid off in September so far, and investors have started reading such cuts as an AI productivity story rather than a distress signal. Khosrowshahi himself has pointed to real tailwinds in productivity from AI.His argument is that acting early beats reacting late. Uber made the cuts from a position of strength rather than weakness, he said, adding that some companies wait and Uber does not believe in waiting. Riders will test that claim the next time they open the app and look at the price.Get the latest technology news and updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: Fresh Houthi attacks injure 13 civilians in Saudi Arabia
articles.summary: The Houthi militia has launched fresh attacks on Saudi Arabia, injuring 13 civilians, officials said on Tuesday. The Iran-backed militia launched drone and m...
articles.body:
Houthi militia launches drone and missile attacks on Saudi Arabia, injuring 13 civilians, prompting fresh warnings from civil defense agency.

Saudi Air Force carries out over 50 airstrikes in Yemen, resulting in three deaths and two injuries, as conflict between Saudi-led coalition and Houthi forces escalates.

United Nations reports 125,000 people displaced in region since start of recent fighting, as Yemeni government continues to target Houthi militia.

The Houthi militia has launched fresh attacks on Saudi Arabia, injuring 13 civilians, officials said on Tuesday.

The Iran-backed militia launched drone and missile attacks on Khamis Mushait, Abha and Taif in the south of Saudi Arabia, said Turki al-Maliki, who serves as the spokesman for the military coalition fighting alongside the Yemeni government against the Houthis.

Saudi Arabia's civil defence agency issued fresh warnings on Tuesday regarding potential threats in Abha and Khamis Mushait. Temporary warnings were also issued for the coastal city of Jeddah on the Red Sea and for al-Ula in the north of the country. No details were initially available regarding possible casualties or damage.

The kingdom had endured one of its "most difficult nights," the Houthi television channel Al-Masirah reported. The Houthis' "major operation" now extends deep into the neighbouring country, where "growing panic" prevails, Al-Masirah said.

The Houthis said there had also been fresh airstrikes by the Saudi Air Force in Yemen. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the Saudi Air Force had carried out more than 50 airstrikes in the provinces of Tais and Marib within 24 hours. The SABA news agency, which is controlled by the militia, reported that three people were killed and two others injured in Saudi airstrikes.

Yemen's internationally recognized government also stated that it had continued to attack Houthi targets and released videos of the latest attacks involving artillery and drones.

The United Nations estimates that 125,000 people have been displaced since the fighting in the region flared up at the start of the month.

articles.title: Swansea alcohol brand Au Vodka purchased by Sazerac for £300m
articles.summary: International spirits brand Sazerac has completed its purchase of Au Vodka for a reported £300m
articles.body:
US drinks giant Sazerac said it has "big plans" for Au Vodka after completing a takeover reported to value the Welsh business at about £300m.

The Swansea-based vodka brand, known for its gold packaging and viral social media campaigns, was founded by friends Charlie Morgan and Jackson Quinn in 2015.

With investment from DJ Charlie Sloth it enjoyed rapid growth before being formally acquired by one of the world's largest spirits companies.

Financial terms have not been disclosed, but the Reuters news agency reported the deal values Au Vodka at about £300m ($405m).

Sazerac chief executive Jake Wenz said Au had enjoyed a "phenomenal growth trajectory" since it was founded in Swansea.

"Au Vodka is a brand we've long admired," he said.

"What Charlie, Jackson, and Charlie have achieved in just over a decade is spectacular and rare, and we have big plans for Au as we welcome the brand into the Sazerac family."

He said that the deal would strengthen Sazerac's position in the UK while creating "a path for continued global growth" for the vodka maker.

Au Vodka was founded by friends Charlie Morgan and Jackson Quinn, with broadcaster and DJ Charlie Sloth later joining as an investor.

Known for its distinctive bottles and cans, the company built a large following through social media marketing and celebrity collaborations.

It has grown into one of the UK's best-known premium vodka brands, and employs more than 80 people in south Wales.

Morgan said the founders had started the business with "nothing but an idea and a belief that vodka didn't have to be boring".

"We are proud to have built it into one of the most disruptive brands of this generation," he said.

"With Sazerac, Au can be offered to more people, in more markets, faster than we ever could alone."

The acquisition adds Au Vodka to a portfolio of more than 500 brands owned by Sazerac, including BuzzBallz and Southern Comfort.
